A WPS qualified per ASME IX uses GTAW root pass on P-No.8 (316L SS), 2G position, 12 mm thickness. The contractor proposes using this WPS for a 1G, 20 mm thick P-No.8 joint. Which statement is correct?

The WPS covers 1G since ASME IX QW-461 allows any position qualified at 2G to be used in 1G.
The WPS does not cover 20 mm because ASME IX QW-451 limits upward range to 2T (24 mm) only for P-No.8 materials above 19 mm.
The WPS is not applicable; position is an essential variable for GTAW and changing from 2G to 1G requires requalification.
The WPS covers both changes; no action is needed.
The WPS covers 1G since ASME IX QW-461 allows any position qualified at 2G to be used in 1G.

Position is NOT an essential variable for GTAW (QW-256) — 2G covers 1G per QW-461.1. For a 12 mm P-No.8 test coupon, qualified range is 3–24 mm (2T); 20 mm is within range. Both changes are acceptable under the existing WPS. Distractor B misapplies a 19 mm threshold from a different table.

During P91 production welding per SAES-W-011, preheat is found at 175°C at tacking. The minimum preheat for P91 >19 mm is 200°C. The welder reheated, but the ITP hold point for preheat was already signed 30 min earlier at 210°C. What is the correct action?

Accept the tacks; the hold-point record confirms 210°C was achieved before welding.
Issue an NCR, quarantine the tacked joint, verify temperature before resuming, and investigate why temperature dropped below minimum during the hold period.
Convert the hold to a witness point and continue; the specification allows a 25°C field tolerance.
Request the welder re-tack without an NCR since no fusion weld was deposited during the low-temperature event.
Issue an NCR, quarantine the tacked joint, verify temperature before resuming, and investigate why temperature dropped below minimum during the hold period.

A hold-point record is valid only at the time of inspection. Temperature drop during the interval is a nonconformance. Tack welds are production welds under SAES-W-011. No tolerance band exists without documented project deviation. Quarantine prevents further work until disposition.

A welder's WPQ was last verified 7 months ago. The QC Manager states it is still valid since no test failure is recorded. The weld log shows he has been performing only grinding and fit-up for 5 months. What is the inspector's assessment?

Valid — ASME IX QW-322.1 only requires 6-month continuity if the welder uses any welding process, including grinding.
Lapsed — ASME IX QW-322.1 requires the qualified process to have been used within 6 months, grinding and fit-up do not constitute welding.
Valid — the 6-month clock resets upon joining a new project.
Valid — only a log review is needed, not an actual weld test, so continuity is maintained.
Lapsed — ASME IX QW-322.1 requires the qualified process to have been used within 6 months, grinding and fit-up do not constitute welding.

ASME IX QW-322.1: welder must have deposited weld metal using the qualified process. Grinding and fit-up are not welding. A 5-month gap without welding activity within the 6-month window lapses the WPQ.

An RT film of a butt weld (ASME B31.3 Normal Fluid Service, 12 mm wall) shows a linear indication 4 mm long at the weld root that cannot be distinguished as slag or lack of fusion by RT alone. What is the correct disposition?

Accept — 4 mm is below the 6 mm maximum slag inclusion length in ASME B31.3 Table 341.3.2.
Reject — any linear indication at the root suspected of being lack of fusion must be treated as the more severe defect type.
Perform supplementary UT to confirm the nature of the indication before final disposition.
Consult the welding engineer and accept provisionally if indication length is less than 1/3 of weld thickness.
Reject — any linear indication at the root suspected of being lack of fusion must be treated as the more severe defect type.

ASME B31.3 requires LOF to be rejected regardless of size. When RT cannot distinguish slag from LOF, conservative characterisation as LOF is mandatory. Applying slag acceptance criteria to an indeterminate indication is non-conservative and non-code-compliant.

SAES-W-011 requires PMI for all P5 chrome-moly filler materials. An E9018-B3 electrode passes XRF, but the XRF calibration label expired 3 days ago. What action should the QC Inspector take?

Accept the PMI results — 3-day expiry is within the typical ±1 week grace period for field instruments.
Reject the PMI results, quarantine tested electrodes, re-calibrate the XRF against a certified reference, and retest all electrodes verified since the last confirmed calibration date.
Accept — XRF drift over 3 days is negligible for alloy content verification.
Request the filler material MTC as a substitute for PMI.
Reject the PMI results, quarantine tested electrodes, re-calibrate the XRF against a certified reference, and retest all electrodes verified since the last confirmed calibration date.

An expired calibration certificate invalidates all readings taken after expiry. No grace period exists unless explicitly stated in the approved inspection procedure. Quarantine scope extends back to the last confirmed valid calibration date. The MTC is not a substitute for in-situ PMI.

The WPS is applicable — repair depth is not an essential variable under ASME IX.
The WPS is not applicable — a repair exceeding 50% through-wall on P91 requires a dedicated repair WPS with full-thickness test coupon and evaluation of temper-bead techniques.

Repair depth >50% through-wall on creep-resistant alloys mandates evaluation of temper-bead welding or full-thickness repair qualification per SAES-W-011. The original WPS does not cover a 14 mm repair on a 20 mm wall.

No — FCAW is a different process from SMAW and is a separate essential variable requiring its own WPQ.

No — FCAW is a different process from SMAW and is a separate essential variable requiring its own WPQ.

Accept — fillet size 5 mm exceeds the pipe wall of 4 mm, meeting the minimum size requirement.
Issue an NCR — ASME B31.3 para 328.5.2 requires ~1.5 mm gap between pipe end and socket bottom, full insertion is a nonconformance.

Accept — 720°C meets both ASME code minimum (620°C) and project specification minimum (720°C).

Accept — RT acceptance confirms weld quality and the WPS has since been approved.
Issue an NCR — the weld was executed without a valid approved WPS, regardless of acceptable RT results.

Apply 100°C preheat — the 0.03 difference in CE is within typical material variability tolerance.
Hold welding and issue an NCR — actual CE exceeds the WPS preheat threshold, this WPS cannot be used without revision or replacement.
Preheat to 150°C as a conservative field adjustment without revising the WPS.

Hold welding and issue an NCR — actual CE exceeds the WPS preheat threshold, this WPS cannot be used without revision or replacement.

An RT film of a 16 mm girth weld (ASME B31.3 Normal Fluid Service) shows a 3.5 mm diameter circular indication. The radiographer classifies it as isolated porosity. What is the correct acceptance determination?

Reject — isolated porosity exceeding 3 mm diameter is always rejected under B31.3 regardless of wall thickness.
Accept — the pore is below the 6 mm maximum diameter limit and less than 1/4T (4 mm), meeting both criteria.
Accept — 3.5 mm is less than 1/4T (4 mm) only, which is the sole criterion.
Reject — B31.3 requires all porosity to be evaluated under ASME V Article 2 technique requirements before any acceptance.
Accept — the pore is below the 6 mm maximum diameter limit and less than 1/4T (4 mm), meeting both criteria.

ASME B31.3 Table 341.3.2 accepts rounded indications up to 1/4T or 6 mm, whichever is less. 1/4T of 16 mm = 4 mm. The 3.5 mm pore is below both limits — acceptable. Distractor A invents a 3 mm blanket rejection rule.

A low-hydrogen E7018 electrode has been in the welder's quiver for 3 hours 55 minutes. The project maximum out-of-oven holding time is 4 hours. The crew supervisor says to continue welding. What is the correct action?

Continue — 5 minutes margin is negligible, electrodes are typically acceptable up to 8 hours in the field.
Stop the welder — at 3 hrs 55 min the electrode will exceed the 4-hour limit before the pass is complete, return it to the oven for reconditioning.
Continue — the 4-hour limit applies to the completed weld, not to each electrode individually.
Accept and document the time deviation in the daily weld log.
Stop the welder — at 3 hrs 55 min the electrode will exceed the 4-hour limit before the pass is complete, return it to the oven for reconditioning.

The 4-hour limit is absolute per AWS A5.1 and the project specification. Starting a weld pass that will not be completed before the limit is exceeded is procedurally unsound. Return the electrode for reconditioning.

No — the 8-inch pipe requires a separate OD qualification test per ASME IX QW-452.
Yes — 6G covers all positions and the OD range ≥25 mm OD is unlimited above the test pipe diameter per ASME IX QW-452.
No — the welder must test on 8-inch pipe because thermal mass difference creates different metallurgical conditions.
Yes — but a supplementary test on 8-inch pipe is required for ARAMCO projects per SAES-W-011.
Yes — 6G covers all positions and the OD range ≥25 mm OD is unlimited above the test pipe diameter per ASME IX QW-452.

During FCAW of A36 structural steel per AWS D1.1, the interpass temperature is 320°C. The WPS maximum is 250°C. The supervisor argues that AWS D1.1 prequalification does not limit interpass temperature for A36. What is correct?

The supervisor is correct — AWS D1.1 prequalified WPS for A36 does not specify an interpass limit; 320°C is acceptable.
The inspector is correct — the approved WPS maximum of 250°C governs even if the code has no default limit for A36.
The supervisor is correct — interpass temperature limits apply only to steels above 70 ksi yield.
Raise a technical query and allow welding to continue pending resolution.
The inspector is correct — the approved WPS maximum of 250°C governs even if the code has no default limit for A36.

The project-specific approved WPS is always controlling. Even where a code has no default interpass limit, if the WPS specifies one it is binding. The inspector must halt welding until temperature returns to ≤250°C.

Reject — undercut depth of 0.8 mm exceeds the B31.3 limit of 0.5 mm (1/64 in) for any wall thickness condition.

Accept — E316L by definition has 4–10 FN; the MTC value may be a minor transcription error.
Reject the batch, quarantine, issue an NCR, and notify procurement — delta ferrite <4 FN is non-compliant with SAES-W-011 regardless of electrode designation.

Accept — ASME B31.3 has no hardness limit for P5B HAZ after PWHT.
Issue an NCR and reject the weld — HV10 285 exceeds the 248 limit, investigate PWHT adequacy and assess repair options including re-PWHT.
Conduct additional hardness tests at 5 more locations before making a disposition.

Issue an NCR and reject the weld — HV10 285 exceeds the 248 limit, investigate PWHT adequacy and assess repair options including re-PWHT.

No issue — the yoke lifts 4.5 kg which meets the minimum, the yoke type is a minor administrative detail.

The AC minimum of 4.5 kg (10 lb) is correctly met, but if the yoke is actually a DC type, the minimum must be 18 kg (40 lb), yoke type must be confirmed and documented.

100% RT per ASME B31.3 Table 341.3.2 for all butt welds in Category D.

A WPQT root bend test specimen for a 2G pipe weld shows a 4.2 mm crack on the tension surface. The bend radius was correct. What is the disposition per ASME IX QW-163?

Pass — 4.2 mm crack is within the 6 mm acceptance criterion in ASME IX QW-163 for root bend tests.
Fail — the 4.2 mm crack exceeds the 3 mm (1/8 in) maximum allowed per ASME IX QW-163, the welder must retest.
Fail — any crack on the tension surface is an automatic failure regardless of length.
Pass — root bend specimens have a separate acceptance criterion of 6 mm for pipe welds.
Fail — the 4.2 mm crack exceeds the 3 mm (1/8 in) maximum allowed per ASME IX QW-163, the welder must retest.

During a hydrostatic hold at 1.5× design pressure (test pressure 15 bar) for 10 minutes, pressure drops from 15 bar to 14.8 bar after 8 minutes. The supervisor says 0.2 bar is within tolerance. What is the correct action?

Accept — a 0.2 bar drop represents less than 2% pressure loss, within ASME B31.3 hydrostatic test tolerance.
Fail the test — any pressure drop during the hold period requires investigation before acceptance, no pressure loss tolerance is defined in B31.3 for hydrostatic testing.
Continue to 10 minutes, if pressure stabilises, accept — the initial drop may be due to temperature equalisation.
Extend the hold to 20 minutes to compensate for minor pressure variation.
Fail the test — any pressure drop during the hold period requires investigation before acceptance, no pressure loss tolerance is defined in B31.3 for hydrostatic testing.
ASME B31.3 para 345.4.2 requires the system to maintain test pressure without leakage for the hold period. No pressure loss tolerance is codified. A pressure drop must be investigated for leakage.

Automated orbital GTAW of 316L SS tubing requires <20 ppm oxygen back-purge before root pass. The purge monitor reads 150 ppm. The crew wants to begin welding. What is the correct action?

Begin welding — 150 ppm is below the 500 ppm threshold typically accepted for SS purging.
Hold welding — 316L requires <20 ppm oxygen before root pass to prevent sensitisation and root oxidation (sugaring), 150 ppm is unacceptable.
Begin welding — oxygen measurement is only a post-weld quality check, not a pre-weld hold.
Hold welding — SAES-W-011 requires 0 ppm oxygen for all SS back-purge before welding begins.
Hold welding — 316L requires <20 ppm oxygen before root pass to prevent sensitisation and root oxidation (sugaring), 150 ppm is unacceptable.

Oxygen content >20–50 ppm during SS GTAW root pass causes oxidation (sugaring), leading to intergranular corrosion. Industry best practice and SAES-W-011 require <20 ppm before commencing root pass. 150 ppm is well above this threshold.

A P91 girth weld cools to ambient temperature during a 35-minute safety evacuation. The WPS requires 200°C minimum preheat and 300°C maximum interpass. Upon return, the supervisor instructs the welder to reheat and continue. What must the QC Inspector verify first?

Verify only that preheat is restored to ≥200°C at the joint before the next pass.
Verify preheat restoration to ≥200°C, inspect the partially completed weld by PT or MT for hydrogen-induced cracking developed during uncontrolled cool-down, and confirm WPS compliance for restart.
Verify preheat only — P91 does not crack during short interruptions if PWHT will follow.
Verify preheat and update the weld traveler; no NDT is needed unless visible cracks are present.
Verify preheat restoration to ≥200°C, inspect the partially completed weld by PT or MT for hydrogen-induced cracking developed during uncontrolled cool-down, and confirm WPS compliance for restart.

Uncontrolled cooling of a partially completed P91 weld creates significant hydrogen cold cracking risk. Simply reheating and continuing without intermediate NDT is inadequate. SAES-W-011 requires inspection of the exposed weld surface before the next pass after an unplanned cool-down.

An RT film of a pressure vessel shell seam (ASME VIII Div.1, 18 mm wall) shows a cluster of three pores — 3 mm, 2.5 mm, and 2 mm diameter — within a 12 mm band. What is the correct assessment?

Accept — all individual pore diameters are below 6 mm and below 1/4T (4.5 mm for this weld).
Reject — the cluster must be evaluated per ASME VIII Div.1 Appendix 4 porosity chart, and this cluster density is likely to exceed the chart allowable.
Accept — ASME VIII permits any number of rounded indications if no single indication exceeds 1/3T.
Reject — ASME VIII mandates rejection of all porosity clusters without exception.
Reject — the cluster must be evaluated per ASME VIII Div.1 Appendix 4 porosity chart, and this cluster density is likely to exceed the chart allowable.

ASME VIII Div.1 App. 4 uses a porosity density chart that evaluates accumulated porosity within a reference length. A 3+2.5+2 mm cluster in 12 mm length must be plotted against the chart — using single-indication B31.3-style logic is inapplicable to ASME VIII pressure vessels.

Accept — E7018-H4 and E7018-H4R are identical, 'R' is a packaging code only.
Reject — E7018-H4R designates moisture-resistant electrodes (≤10 ml/100g after 9 hr exposure at 27°C/80% RH per AWS A5.1), without 'R', moisture resistance is unverified and the electrode does not meet the WPS requirement.
Accept — H4 hydrogen designation is the controlling requirement, moisture resistance is a supplemental commercial designation.
Reject — E7018-H4R is required only for weld repairs, not production welds.

Reject — E7018-H4R designates moisture-resistant electrodes (≤10 ml/100g after 9 hr exposure at 27°C/80% RH per AWS A5.1), without 'R', moisture resistance is unverified and the electrode does not meet the WPS requirement.

For a DN50 nozzle-to-shell connection, ASME VIII Div.1 UW-11 requires only visual inspection if the vessel is not in the fully radiographed category.

For a DN50 nozzle-to-shell connection, ASME VIII Div.1 UW-11 requires only visual inspection if the vessel is not in the fully radiographed category.

A pipe-to-pipe girth weld fit-up (ASME B31.3) shows internal misalignment of 2.0 mm on an 8 mm wall pipe. ASME B31.3 para 328.4.2 limits hi-lo to 1.5 mm or 1/4T, whichever is less. What is the finding?

Accept — 2.0 mm misalignment is within the 2 mm hi-lo commonly accepted in ARAMCO field practice.
Reject — 2.0 mm exceeds the governing limit of 1.5 mm (which is less than 1/4T = 2 mm), re-fit-up is required.
Accept — 2.0 mm equals 1/4 × 8 mm = 2 mm and is within one of the two acceptance criteria.
Reject only if the misalignment is detectable on the RT film.
Reject — 2.0 mm exceeds the governing limit of 1.5 mm (which is less than 1/4T = 2 mm), re-fit-up is required.

The limit is 1.5 mm or 1/4T, whichever is LESS. 1/4T = 2 mm; 1.5 mm < 2 mm; therefore 1.5 mm governs. 2.0 mm > 1.5 mm → reject fit-up. Distractor C misapplies 'whichever is less' to mean either criterion can be used.

83 bar — ASME B31.3 para 345.4.2 requires 1.5× design pressure multiplied by the allowable stress ratio (σ at ambient / σ at design temperature) when the ratio exceeds 1.0.
62.5 bar — ASME B31.3 para 345.4.2 requires 1.25× design pressure for systems at elevated temperatures.

ASME B31.3 para 345.4.2: minimum test pressure = 1.5 × P × (St/S) where St = allowable stress at test temperature (ambient) and S = allowable stress at design temperature. Explain the difference between a hydrostatic test and a pneumatic leak test — when is each used, and what are the safety implications of each?

Grade on: Hydrostatic — uses water (incompressible), higher stored energy efficiency, safe failure mode (no explosion energy), ASME B31.3 default; Pneumatic — uses gas (compressible, high stored energy), explosive failure mode, used only when hydrostatic is impractical (damage to lining, residual liquid hazard), requires exclusion zone and safety plan, lower test pressure (1.1× vs. 1.5×). Safety implication: pneumatic failure releases enormous energy; hydrostatic failure is typically a controlled leak.

The contractor wants to use a ball valve as an isolation device for the hydrostatic test boundary. You know that ball valves are not reliable test boundary devices. How do you handle this?

Grade on: Test boundary isolation must use spades/blinds (blank flanges) — a ball valve is not a positive isolation device for testing purposes (valve seats can leak under test pressure, pressure can bypass through valve body, valve may not be rated for the test pressure condition); explain technically that ASME B31.3 and the test package require blind flanges as test boundaries; insist on the correct hardware; do not approve the test boundary with a valve-only isolation.

Explain what an eccentric reducer is, why 'flat on top' orientation matters, and give an example of when 'flat on bottom' would be specified instead.

Grade on: Eccentric reducer has centreline offset between the two ends; flat on top — the top of the pipe stays level, preventing gas pockets in liquid-filled lines (used in liquid process lines where gas pockets cause flow measurement errors and cavitation); flat on bottom — the bottom of the pipe stays level, preventing liquid slugging in gas lines and avoiding cavitation on pump suction (pump suction reducers are flat-on-bottom to maintain steady liquid fill to the impeller and avoid vapour lock).

During a routine walk-down you notice a piping crew using an adjustable spanner (crescent wrench) to torque a flange bolt on a Class 600 hydrocarbon flange. What is your reaction and why?

Grade on: Stop the work immediately — adjustable spanners apply arbitrary, uncontrolled torque and can over-torque bolts (damaging gaskets, stretching bolts) or under-torque bolts (leak risk); Class 600 hydrocarbon flanges require controlled torque application using a calibrated torque wrench or hydraulic bolt tensioner; document the incident; determine which flanges were tightened with this method and require full re-torquing with the correct tool; issue a toolbox talk on correct practices.

Explain what CUI (Corrosion Under Insulation) is and describe three design/construction measures that reduce CUI risk in a piping system.

Grade on: CUI — corrosion that occurs on the external surface of a pipe beneath insulation, caused by ingress of water (rain, steam leaks, process leaks) that cannot easily evaporate and becomes trapped; temperature range of concern: −4°C to 175°C for CS (austenitic SS susceptible to Cl-SCC between 50–175°C); design/construction measures: (1) use pipe shoes at all support points to prevent water entrapment; (2) use weather-resistant insulation jacketing (aluminium, SS) with sealed joints; (3) weep holes at all support gusset plates; (4) correct insulation end-seal details at flanges and valves; (5) avoid horizontal supports without drainage.

You are reviewing an isometric drawing for a critical high-pressure CS piping system and notice the drawing has no revision history or revision number. The drawing was used for fabrication. What are the implications?

Grade on: An uncontrolled drawing (no revision history) may not be the latest approved version; fabrication from a superseded drawing can result in dimensional errors, wrong specifications, or incorrect materials; implications: the fabricated spool must be verified against the confirmed latest approved isometric; if a revision exists that the fabricator was unaware of, NCR and assessment are required; corrective action for document control system to prevent unapproved drawings reaching the shop floor.

Explain why it is important to verify that a valve is installed in the correct flow direction — give two examples of valve types where direction is critical.

Grade on: Flow direction determines valve function; Examples: (1) Check valve — must face in the direction of permitted forward flow; installed backwards, it fails to prevent backflow (the primary function); (2) Control valve — many control valve bodies are directional; installed backwards, the valve may not regulate correctly, cavitate, or produce excessive pressure drop in the wrong location; (3) Globe valve — installed backwards (flow under disk) may cause seat erosion; (4) Wafer butterfly valve — some designs are asymmetric and must face the pipe flow direction for correct seating.

A field engineer asks you as the QC inspector to sign off a piping spool that is not in your ITP scope. He says it's a routine utility line and the TPIA didn't show up. How do you handle this?

Grade on: The QC inspector cannot sign off work outside their defined scope in the ITP without prior authorisation; explain to the field engineer that signing off work outside the ITP scope is itself a quality system nonconformance; the correct action is to notify the QC Manager, who can either (a) confirm the TPIA's absence was notified and agreed per the ITP procedure, or (b) arrange for the TPIA to attend; if the TPIA hold point can be waived with proper documentation, this must be done formally — not by having the QC inspector sign in place of the TPIA.

Explain the concept of 'stress corrosion cracking' (SCC) and identify two service environments in a piping system where SCC is a significant concern.

Grade on: SCC — corrosion mechanism that requires the simultaneous presence of three conditions: (1) susceptible material, (2) tensile stress (residual or applied), (3) specific corrosive environment; the crack propagates under combined stress and corrosion even though neither alone would cause rapid failure; Examples: (1) Austenitic SS (304/316) in chloride-containing environments — Cl-SCC at >60°C; (2) Carbon steel in caustic (NaOH) — caustic SCC (stress corrosion cracking also called caustic embrittlement); (3) Carbon/low-alloy steel in wet H₂S — sulfide stress cracking (SSC); (4) Duplex SS in polythionic acid environments during shutdowns.

You arrive to inspect a line flushing operation and notice the operator is flushing a stainless steel process line with portable water from a garden hose. The water source is not the approved demineralised water specified in the flushing procedure. What do you do?

Grade on: Stop the flushing immediately — potable water contains chlorides (typically 50–250 ppm Cl) that remain on the pipe surface after drying and can initiate chloride stress corrosion cracking in stainless steel under operating conditions; the flush must be completed using demineralised or distilled water as specified; the line must be inspected for residual contamination (Cl test strips if already flushed with potable water); issue NCR; corrective action for flushing medium control.

What is the purpose of a spectacle blind (figure-8 blind) in piping, and how does it differ from a spade and a spacer ring?

Grade on: Spectacle blind — a figure-8 shaped fitting with one solid half (blind) and one open ring half (spacer); it can be rotated to switch between isolated (blind side in) and open (spacer side in) configurations, with the position visible externally; Spade — solid disc only (blind); used for long-term isolation; Spacer — open ring only; keeps flanges at full bolt length when the blind is not in use; Practical use: spectacle blinds are ideal for operations that regularly switch between isolated and normal flow, providing clear visual indication of blind status — critical for safety permit-to-work systems.

Describe the sequence of events that should happen when a pressure test fails — who gets notified, what documentation is generated, and how is the repair managed?

Grade on: Sequence: (1) Depressurise safely per test procedure; (2) Notify: QC Manager, Construction Manager, TPIA inspector, ARAMCO resident engineer; (3) Issue NCR documenting the test failure, observed symptoms, and location of leak (if found); (4) Investigate root cause — find leak location, characterise failure (fabrication defect, wrong material, missing seal, etc.); (5) Develop repair plan (weld repair, gasket replacement, valve replacement); (6) Implement repair under normal QC hold-point regime; (7) Repeat pressure test; (8) Document test repeat and acceptance; NCR formally closed with evidence.

Explain the difference between a butt weld fitting and a socket weld fitting — when would you use each, and what are the ASME B31.3 restrictions on socket welds?

Grade on: Butt weld — pipe ends meet face-to-face with a full-penetration groove weld; provides full bore with no step; used for all sizes in critical service; inspectable by RT/UT; Socket weld — pipe slips into the fitting socket; sealed by fillet weld only; creates a crevice at the pipe-socket junction; limited to NPS ≤ 2 inch per ASME B31.3; not permitted in severe cyclic service; crevice makes RT of root impossible; used for small bore less critical applications.

During a hydrostatic test walk-down, you notice a pressure gauge has a cracked lens (the glass face is cracked but the needle is visible). The gauge is being used to monitor test pressure. What is your action?

Grade on: Stop and replace the gauge — a cracked lens is a safety hazard (the glass can shatter under pressure, injuring personnel) and an instrumentation integrity concern (the crack may have been caused by over-pressure, suggesting the gauge mechanism may be damaged and reading incorrectly); replace with a calibrated gauge with current calibration sticker; investigate whether over-pressure may have occurred; record the replacement in the test documentation.

A construction crew is about to install pipe in a trench. You observe the trench bottom has standing water and the bedding material is coarse gravel (instead of the specified fine sand). The pipe is FBE-coated. What are your concerns and actions?

Grade on: Two concerns: (1) Coarse gravel bedding will damage the FBE coating — hard angular gravel contacts create stress concentration points that chip or penetrate the coating; fine sand/granular fill is specified to protect the coating; (2) Standing water in the trench — laying pipe in water risks coating damage, weld contamination, and improper bedding compaction; Actions: stop pipe installation; require dewatering before placement; require replacement of coarse gravel with specified fine sand/granular fill per SAES coating specification; inspect the FBE coating after bedding correction for any damage using holiday detector.

You receive a hydrostatic test package for a 4-inch Class 600 CS process piping system. The test data shows: Design pressure 50 bar, design temperature 300°C, allowable stress at 300°C (S) = 117 MPa, allowable stress at ambient (St) = 138 MPa. Calculate the minimum required test pressure per ASME B31.3 para 345.4.2 and state whether the proposed test pressure of 90 bar is acceptable.

Grade on: Formula: Pt = 1.5 × P × (St/S) = 1.5 × 50 × (138/117) = 75 × 1.179 = 88.4 bar minimum. Proposed test pressure = 90 bar. 90 bar > 88.4 bar — ACCEPTABLE. Candidate must correctly apply the stress ratio correction; the common error is calculating 1.5 × 50 = 75 bar without the temperature correction factor.

Review the following flange inspection record and identify any discrepancies: Flange A (6-inch Class 300 RF): Gasket type — spiral-wound SS/PTFE; Face finish measured — 3.2 μm Ra (specified ASME B16.5 range 3.2–6.3 μm Ra for spiral-wound gaskets); Two radial scratches 0.1 mm deep, 30 mm long across the raised face; Bolts — A193 B7 studs with A194 2H nuts (correct per specification); Torque — 180 Nm (single pass).

Grade on: (1) Gasket type — spiral-wound SS/PTFE for Class 300 RF — ACCEPTABLE (verify inner ring required for Class ≥300 per ASME B16.20); (2) Face finish 3.2 μm Ra — at the lower boundary of the acceptable range (3.2–6.3 μm Ra for ASME B16.5 with spiral-wound gasket) — borderline ACCEPTABLE; (3) Two radial scratches 0.1 mm deep across the raised face — REJECT — radial scratches are leak paths, must be re-machined; (4) Bolt material — correct; (5) Torque — 180 Nm single pass — REJECT per ASME PCC-1 — must be progressive cross-pattern torquing (30%, 70%, 100%). Two NCR items.

practical

Calculate the remaining life and next inspection date for the following API 570 data: Current wall thickness = 6.8 mm; Minimum required thickness = 4.5 mm; Corrosion rate (short-term) = 0.6 mm/yr; Corrosion rate (long-term) = 0.4 mm/yr. API 570 requires using the higher of the two rates. State the remaining life and next inspection interval.

Grade on: Use the higher corrosion rate = 0.6 mm/yr. Remaining life = (6.8 − 4.5) / 0.6 = 2.3 / 0.6 = 3.83 years. Next inspection interval per API 570 = half the remaining life = 1.92 years (approximately 23 months). The inspection must also not exceed the maximum allowed interval per API 570 for the risk category (typically 10 years for external, 5 years for internal — but remaining life governs here). Next inspection due in approximately 1.9 years.

A contractor submits a flange bolt torque calculation for 8-inch Class 600 ANSI flanges using A193 B7 stud bolts, spiral-wound gasket with inner ring. They calculated a target torque of 340 Nm. During your review you note: bolt size is 7/8-inch diameter, number of bolts is 12, and the calculation uses a K-factor (nut factor) of 0.2. A colleague says the K-factor should be 0.15 for lubricated bolts with Molykote. Evaluate the torque calculation sensitivity to this K-factor difference.

Grade on: Torque T = K × F × D, where K = nut factor, F = bolt load, D = nominal bolt diameter. The K-factor directly and linearly affects the required torque — a K of 0.15 vs. 0.20 changes torque by (0.15/0.20) = 75%; if 340 Nm was calculated at K=0.20 with Molykote (which should use K=0.15), the actual torque achieves a 33% HIGHER bolt load than intended (same torque, lower K = more preload). Conversely, if K=0.15 is correct, using K=0.20 torque would underload the bolts. The calculation should use the K-factor for the actual lubricant applied. This is a design issue requiring engineering clarification and revision of the torque procedure with the correct K-factor.

During line flushing of a new 6-inch CS process line, the flushing team reports that water exiting from the downstream flush point is milky white and turbid. The line was internally pickled with citric acid solution before flushing. Evaluate the flushing status and state what action is required.

Grade on: Milky white turbid water after citric acid pickling can indicate: (1) Residual acid reacting with pipe scale or iron oxide, producing iron citrate compounds; (2) Insufficient rinsing — acid not fully displaced; (3) Possible surface passivation reaction products; Action required: Continue flushing with clean water until the outlet runs clear and pH matches the inlet flush water pH (within ±0.5 pH); test pH and conductivity of flushing water outlet; if still turbid after extended flushing, investigate whether pickling solution concentration or contact time was correct; do not place line in service until flushing water is clear and meets acceptance criteria (pH, conductivity, turbidity).

A piping inspection report shows a 3-inch SS316L pipe elbow at a dead-leg junction in a pharmaceutical utility (high-purity water, USP grade) service. The elbow creates a dead-leg of 350 mm length from the last T-junction. The project specification states dead-legs must not exceed 3× the pipe diameter (3D rule). Evaluate whether this dead-leg is acceptable.

Grade on: 3× pipe diameter rule: pipe ID approximately 73 mm for 3-inch Schedule 10S (OD = 88.9 mm, wall = 2.77 mm, ID ≈ 83.4 mm). 3D = 3 × 83.4 = 250 mm. Dead-leg length = 350 mm. 350 mm > 250 mm — FAIL the 3D rule. The dead-leg exceeds the maximum allowed length. In high-purity water service, excessive dead-legs create stagnant zones where biofilm growth (microbiological contamination) can occur. The piping must be redesigned to shorten the dead-leg or re-route to eliminate it.

You receive a test package for a pneumatic leak test of a completed instrument air distribution ring main (8 bar design pressure, 12 bar test pressure). During RT of a 25 mm wall pressure vessel weld (ASME VIII Div.1), the radiographer places the IQI on the source side. The procedure requires source-side IQI placement. The IQI image is visible on the film. However, no shim was placed under the IQI and the IQI is directly on the weld crown. What is the technical concern?

The IQI placed directly on the weld crown will produce an artificially better sensitivity reading because the IQI is at a thicker section of the part.
The IQI placed on the weld crown is at a raised area, without a shim equal to the weld crown height, the IQI hole image represents a sensitivity level achieved through the weld crown, not through the full 25 mm base metal — the true sensitivity at the base metal section is unverified.
No concern — ASME V requires IQI placement on the highest point of the part for worst-case sensitivity assessment.
The IQI should be placed on the film side for maximum sensitivity verification.

The IQI placed on the weld crown is at a raised area, without a shim equal to the weld crown height, the IQI hole image represents a sensitivity level achieved through the weld crown, not through the full 25 mm base metal — the true sensitivity at the base metal section is unverified.

ASME V T-277.1(a): a shim equal to the maximum weld crown height must be placed under the IQI when placed on the crown, so the IQI is exposed through material of the same total thickness as the weld. Without the shim, the IQI is exposed through greater thickness (crown + base), yielding an artificially better (thicker) sensitivity value than the base metal area actually receives.

An RT technician performs a radiograph and the resulting film has a density of 1.5 H&D in the area of interest. The procedure requires 1.8–4.0 H&D. The technician argues that 1.5 H&D is conservative because the film is lighter and easier to see through. What is the correct assessment?

Accept — lighter films are always easier to interpret, a density of 1.5 H&D improves image quality.
Reject — 1.5 H&D is below the minimum 1.8 H&D, low density means insufficient contrast for reliable defect detection, the film must be retaken at increased exposure.
Accept — ASME V density requirements are guidelines, not hard limits.
Accept — a density of 1.5 H&D is acceptable at the edges of the radiation cone due to reduced scatter.
Reject — 1.5 H&D is below the minimum 1.8 H&D, low density means insufficient contrast for reliable defect detection, the film must be retaken at increased exposure.

Low film density (too light) reduces contrast and makes it harder to detect small indications — the lower density limit is not a conservative acceptance criterion. The physical darkening of film creates the contrast difference between defects and the background. Below 1.8 H&D, film contrast is insufficient for reliable interpretation. The film must be retaken.

During PAUT (Phased Array UT) examination of a 20 mm wall pipe weld, the technician uses a reference block of the same material, thickness, and surface condition. A side-drilled hole (SDH) at 2/3 depth (13.3 mm from surface) is used as the primary reference reflector. The DAC curve is set at 80% FSH from this reflector. An indication is detected at 50% FSH. What is the correct recording and reporting requirement?

The indication at 50% FSH is below the DAC and does not need to be recorded.
The indication at 50% FSH is above the 20% FSH recording threshold (25% of DAC) and must be recorded in the UT report with location, depth, and amplitude.
The indication at 50% FSH is above the 50% FSH characterisation threshold and must be sized and reported.
The indication at 50% FSH represents 62.5% of DAC; all indications ≥20% of DAC must be recorded.
The indication at 50% FSH is above the 20% FSH recording threshold (25% of DAC) and must be recorded in the UT report with location, depth, and amplitude.

ASME V Article 4 UT: recording threshold is typically ≥20% FSH (25% of 80% DAC reference). 50% FSH > 20% recording threshold — must be recorded. It is below 80% (100% DAC) rejection level, so it is not automatically rejected, but it requires documentation for characterisation evaluation. Distractor A incorrectly applies the rejection threshold as the recording threshold.

A Liquid Penetrant Test (PT) procedure per ASME V Article 6 requires a minimum dwell time of 10 minutes for the penetrant application step on a carbon steel plate with a design temperature of 50°C. The ambient temperature is 45°C. The surface temperature of the plate is measured at 43°C. Is the procedure still applicable?

Yes — 43°C is close enough to 45°C ambient and within the typical instrument tolerance.
No — ASME V T-652 requires the part temperature to be between 4°C and 52°C for standard aqueous visible PT, 43°C is within this range. However, the examiner should verify whether the dwell time needs to be adjusted for the elevated part temperature.
No — ASME V Article 6 prohibits PT on surfaces above 40°C to prevent premature evaporation of penetrant.
Yes — the ambient temperature governs dwell time, not surface temperature.

No — ASME V T-652 requires the part temperature to be between 4°C and 52°C for standard aqueous visible PT, 43°C is within this range. However, the examiner should verify whether the dwell time needs to be adjusted for the elevated part temperature.

ASME V T-652 temperature range for PT is 4°C–52°C (40°F–125°F). At 43°C (well above 38°C), the penetrant may evaporate faster and dwell time adjustments or a higher-viscosity penetrant may be required. During MT (Magnetic Particle Inspection) of a weld using the continuous method per ASME V Article 7, the technician applies the magnetic particles before the magnetising current is energised, then energises the current. What is the nonconformance?

No nonconformance — particles can be applied before or after energising the current per ASME V.
Nonconformance — the continuous method requires the magnetic particles to be applied WHILE the magnetising current is energised, applying particles before magnetisation means the particles are not being drawn to leakage flux at active indication sites.
Nonconformance — the particles must be applied after the current is shut off, not before.
No nonconformance — the sequence of particle application relative to current is at the technician's discretion.

Nonconformance — the continuous method requires the magnetic particles to be applied WHILE the magnetising current is energised, applying particles before magnetisation means the particles are not being drawn to leakage flux at active indication sites.

ASME V T-745.1 continuous method: magnetising current is applied simultaneously with and continued during particle application. The particles migrate to leakage flux patterns at discontinuities while the field is active. Applying particles before energising the field negates the detection principle — any weak indication sites will not attract particles effectively.

An ASNT Level II UT technician is examining a 50 mm thick weld using a 45° refracted shear wave probe. The technician calibrates using a reference block with a 1.5 mm SDH. During scanning, an indication at the half-skip position of the probe shows a response. Where in the weld is this indication most likely located?

At the weld root (fusion line at the ID surface).
At the mid-wall depth — approximately 25 mm from the scanning surface.
At the weld cap surface (OD).
In the HAZ adjacent to the weld, near the OD surface.
At the weld root (fusion line at the ID surface).

For a 45° shear wave probe on the OD surface of a 50 mm weld, the half-skip position corresponds to the beam reflecting off the ID surface and returning to the mid-path. The beam contacts the ID (weld root) at the half-skip distance. This is the classic 45° shear wave configuration for root area inspection from the OD.

A PT examination using a fluorescent penetrant system (Method A, Type I per ASME V) is being performed in a field environment. The UV-A light intensity at the inspection surface is measured at 850 μW/cm². ASME V T-676.1 requires a minimum of 1000 μW/cm². The technician argues the indication is still visible. What is the correct action?

Accept — indicator visibility is the true criterion for fluorescent MT/PT, not a prescribed UV intensity.
Stop the inspection — UV-A intensity must be ≥1000 μW/cm² per ASME V T-676.1 before any fluorescent PT examination can proceed, all areas inspected with sub-standard UV intensity must be re-examined after increasing the UV output.
Accept with a level of conservatism — 850 μW/cm² is only 15% below minimum and the indication was still detected.
Continue but document the reduced UV intensity and have a Level III review the findings.

Stop the inspection — UV-A intensity must be ≥1000 μW/cm² per ASME V T-676.1 before any fluorescent PT examination can proceed, all areas inspected with sub-standard UV intensity must be re-examined after increasing the UV output.

ASME V T-676.1 minimum UV-A intensity is 1000 μW/cm² (measured at the inspection surface). This is an absolute requirement — argument that 'the indication is still visible' is subjective and non-code. Anything below 1000 μW/cm² invalidates the examination. All previously examined areas must be re-done after correcting the UV source.

A PAUT scan of a dissimilar metal weld (DMW) between carbon steel and Inconel 625 cladding shows a planar indication at the fusion boundary interface. The indication is 18 mm long and through-wall height is estimated at 3 mm by TOFD. The applicable acceptance criterion per ASME VIII Div.2 for surface-connected planar indications allows maximum 1.5 mm through-wall height. What is the disposition?

Accept — the 3 mm height is below the 6 mm maximum for volumetric indications under ASME VIII Div.2.
Reject — 3 mm through-wall height for a surface-connected planar indication exceeds the 1.5 mm maximum, the weld must be repaired.
Request a Level 3 API 579 FFS assessment before rejection.
Accept — the 18 mm length is within the code length acceptance criterion.
Reject — 3 mm through-wall height for a surface-connected planar indication exceeds the 1.5 mm maximum, the weld must be repaired.

ASME VIII Div.2 Chapter 7 acceptance criteria for surface-connected planar indications specify strict through-wall height limits. A 3 mm height at a fusion boundary (where LOF/bonding defects are service-critical) exceeds the 1.5 mm maximum. The length criterion is applied separately — even a short indication with excessive through-wall height is rejectable.

An RT procedure qualifies Source-to-Film Distance (SFD) of 700 mm for a 12 mm thick weld. A Level III wants to reduce the SFD to 500 mm to improve exposure time on a remote field job. Using ASME V Article 2, what is the minimum SFD requirement to maintain the required geometric unsharpness (Ug ≤ 0.51 mm per ASME V T-274.2)?

No minimum SFD is specified in ASME V — geometric unsharpness must be calculated and confirmed ≤0.51 mm.
SFD must be ≥ 700 mm because the original procedure was qualified at that distance.
SFD can be reduced to 500 mm only if the film-to-object distance is proportionally reduced.
SFD ≥ Source size × (t + d) / Ug, where t = weld thickness and d = source-to-film object distance, the minimum SFD must be calculated using the actual source size to meet Ug ≤0.51 mm.
SFD ≥ Source size × (t + d) / Ug, where t = weld thickness and d = source-to-film object distance, the minimum SFD must be calculated using the actual source size to meet Ug ≤0.51 mm.

ASME V T-274.1 requires Ug ≤ 0.51 mm. Ug = (f × d) / SFD where f = source size (focal spot), d = film-to-object distance. The minimum SFD = f × d / Ug. Reducing SFD to 500 mm requires calculating whether the geometric unsharpness criterion is still met with the specific source size. Simply reducing SFD without recalculation is not permitted.
NDT QC
mcq
During TOFD examination of a 40 mm wall pressure vessel seam weld, the D-scan display shows a parabolic indication at the lateral wave position. This type of indication is most likely caused by:

A through-wall crack perpendicular to the weld axis in the base metal.
A near-surface planar defect at the OD surface, causing diffraction from the defect tips and appearing as a parabolic arc at the lateral wave.
Grain noise from coarse austenitic microstructure reflecting the ultrasonic beam.
A gas pore at mid-wall producing a specular reflection visible in the D-scan.
A near-surface planar defect at the OD surface, causing diffraction from the defect tips and appearing as a parabolic arc at the lateral wave.

In TOFD, indications that appear as hyperbolic or parabolic arcs are caused by point-source diffraction from defect tips. A parabolic arc at or near the lateral wave position indicates the defect is close to the OD surface (near the lateral wave zone). Mid-wall defects appear as arcs between the lateral wave and back wall signal. Grain noise produces a diffuse, non-coherent background.

An ASNT Level II PT technician finds a linear indication 22 mm long on the surface of a CS pressure vessel weld. Per ASME VIII Div.1 Appendix 8, any linear indication is rejectable if its length exceeds 1.5 mm (1/16 in). The technician removes the indication with a wire brush and then reports 'no indication found.' What is the concern?

No concern — removing the indication and reporting clear is an accepted field technique for marginal PT indications.
Major concern — using a wire brush to remove an indication is smearing and masking the defect, the smeared metal fills the surface crack opening, preventing penetrant entry, the weld must be properly excavated, examined by PT after excavation, and if a crack is confirmed, a repair weld performed.
Minor concern — the wire brush may have contaminated the PT developer and the area should be re-cleaned and re-tested.
No concern — the technician is a Level II and has authority to characterise and disposition indications independently.

Major concern — using a wire brush to remove an indication is smearing and masking the defect, the smeared metal fills the surface crack opening, preventing penetrant entry, the weld must be properly excavated, examined by PT after excavation, and if a crack is confirmed, a repair weld performed.

Wire brushing a PT indication is a well-known form of defect masking. The mechanical action smears metal over the crack opening, preventing future penetrant entry. This must be treated as a deliberate or negligent concealment of a defect. The weld must be excavated by grinding to reveal the underlying defect and re-examined. This is also a potential integrity and safety reporting violation.

An RT technician is requested to radiograph a 10-inch Schedule 80 (wall 12.7 mm) CS pipe weld using a single-wall single-image (SWSI) technique per ASME V Article 2. The source is on one side, the film on the other. However, the IQI image on the film shows the penetrameter has rolled off to one side — the IQI is not in the weld area image. What does this indicate?

The IQI is acceptable — it only needs to be present on the film, not necessarily over the weld area.
The IQI is incorrectly placed — the IQI must image within or adjacent to the area of interest on the weld to validate sensitivity in the critical examination zone, the film is invalid and must be retaken.
The IQI is at the source side — rolling is acceptable for source-side IQI placement per ASME V.
The IQI is valid — the sensitivity is uniform across the film when the density is within range.

The IQI is incorrectly placed — the IQI must image within or adjacent to the area of interest on the weld to validate sensitivity in the critical examination zone, the film is invalid and must be retaken.

ASME V T-277.1 requires the IQI to be placed in the area of interest (or on a representative shim adjacent to the weld). If the IQI image is not within the weld examination zone on the film, the required sensitivity at the weld area cannot be confirmed. The film is unacceptable and must be retaken with correct IQI positioning.

500 lux (50 foot-candles) minimum at the inspection surface.
1000 lux (100 foot-candles) minimum at the inspection surface.
2000 lux (200 foot-candles) minimum at the inspection surface.
No minimum is specified — the examiner must be able to resolve a 4:1 black-white line pattern at the inspection distance.
1000 lux (100 foot-candles) minimum at the inspection surface.

ASME V Article 9, T-952: direct visual examination requires minimum illumination of 1000 lux (100 foot-candles) at the inspection surface. The resolution requirement (black-white line pattern) is a separate qualification test for the examiner's visual acuity, not for the lighting level.

Compare the capabilities and limitations of RT vs. PAUT for the following weld defect types: (a) planar defects (LOF, cracks) perpendicular to the weld axis; (b) porosity clusters; (c) root concavity; (d) transverse cracks. Explain which method is superior for each and why.

Grade on: (a) Planar defects perpendicular to weld axis — PAUT superior (can use angle beams perpendicular to defect plane); RT very poor for defects parallel to beam; (b) Porosity clusters — RT superior (volumetric defects show clearly as dark spots on film; PAUT can detect but sizing is less precise); (c) Root concavity — RT superior (geometric feature clearly visible as dark band at root on film; UT angle beam can detect but characterisation less reliable); (d) Transverse cracks — PAUT superior using transverse scanning; RT may miss transverse cracks if beam is parallel to crack plane.

The technician re-scans the area manually and does not detect the indication. He decides to accept the weld based on the manual re-scan. Evaluate this decision and describe the correct procedure.

Grade on: Automated systems flag indications based on programmed acceptance thresholds — automated alarm is evidence-based. Manually re-scanning and overriding an automated alarm with a subjective manual scan is not an accepted disposition method. Correct procedure: preserve the original AUT data file; escalate to Level III for independent data review; if the automated indication is confirmed as an artifact (e.g., geometry noise, transducer lift-off), document the basis for acceptance; if the alarm cannot be confirmed as an artifact, the weld should be rejected and repaired. The technician cannot unilaterally override an automated alarm.

You are leading an NDT quality audit of a contractor's PT operation on stainless steel weld overlays. You observe the following: penetrant applied to a warm surface (38°C); dwell time 7 minutes; water wash at approximately 35°C; developer applied immediately after washing without drying; no UV light illumination (visible PT system). Identify all nonconformances and their implications.

Grade on: (1) Warm surface 38°C — ASME V maximum surface temperature for standard aqueous PT is 52°C; 38°C is within range but may require extended dwell time; (2) Dwell time 7 minutes — verify against procedure requirement (typically ≥10 min for stress corrosion cracking risk areas); (3) Water wash temperature acceptable; (4) Developer applied without drying — water must be removed before developer or the developer will not function correctly; this is a significant nonconformance — the water dilutes and prevents developer formation on the surface; (5) No UV light — visible PT does not need UV; not a violation. Primary nonconformance: developer without drying step. All areas must be re-examined.

Explain the likely cause of each indication, the acceptance criteria, and the disposition of each finding.

Explain in plain language what the IQI (Image Quality Indicator) tells us about an RT film and what it does NOT tell us.

Grade on: IQI tells us: the minimum detectable feature size (sensitivity) achieved in the radiograph — it confirms that features of a certain size (wire diameter or hole diameter) are visible on the film at the examination location; it does NOT tell us: the exact size of a defect, the nature of a defect, whether a specific defect exists, or that the examination is otherwise correctly performed. IQI is a sensitivity indicator, not a defect detector.

A welder argues that his weld has 'perfect' RT films so there cannot be any defects. Explain why this is an oversimplification.

Grade on: RT has limitations — it cannot detect planar defects oriented parallel to the beam (cracks, LOF perpendicular to the film plane); the acceptable criteria per code still allow some embedded defects below rejection limits; RT cannot detect surface-only defects (requires PT/MT); the IQI sensitivity only covers down to the IQI-specified size — defects below this threshold may not be detectable; RT is excellent for volumetric defects (porosity, slag) but limited for planar defects (cracks, LOF).

What is 'Probability of Detection' (POD) in NDT and why does it matter for safety-critical inspection?

Grade on: POD — the statistical likelihood that a specific NDE method and technique will detect a specific defect of a given type, size, and orientation; expressed as a percentage (e.g., 90% POD for a 2 mm crack); matters because: no NDE method has 100% POD — qualified procedures should demonstrate high POD (typically ≥90%) for the target defect size; safety-critical inspections (pressure vessels, pipelines) must be performed with methods validated for adequate POD; if POD is unknown or unvalidated, the inspection provides false confidence in weld acceptance.

You are reviewing RT films and you see an indication that looks like a crack. The Level II technician insists it is a slag inclusion. You disagree. What do you do?

Grade on: The QC Inspector's role is not to override the Level II interpretation but to ensure the process is correct; document your observation formally (mark the film, write in your inspection log); request the Level II technician to document his characterisation basis (density, geometry, location); if disagreement persists, escalate to the Level III NDT engineer for independent review; the weld should be placed on hold pending Level III resolution — do not release the weld while there is an unresolved interpretation dispute.

During a site visit, you observe that the NDT technician is applying PT penetrant and reading the results in direct sunlight on a hot Arabian Gulf summer day. What concerns do you raise?

Grade on: Direct sunlight causes: (1) rapid penetrant evaporation (shortened effective dwell time, penetrant may dry before developer is applied); (2) surface temperature potentially exceeding 52°C — above ASME V maximum for standard penetrant; (3) UV fluorescent PT is impossible in direct sunlight (ambient UV from sun masks fluorescent indications); correct practice: shade the examination area, verify surface temperature, re-read minimum dwell time under controlled conditions, use temperature-appropriate penetrant if surface temperature is confirmed elevated.

What is the 'half-skip' distance in angle beam UT and why is it important for root area inspection?

Grade on: Half-skip = the scanning position of the probe at which the angled beam first contacts the opposite surface (ID surface) of the weld; at this position, the beam has travelled from the OD surface, through the weld, to the ID and is at the reflector position for root area defects (LOF at root, root cracking, incomplete penetration); knowing the half-skip distance allows the technician to position the probe correctly for root examination; the full-skip is twice this distance and is used for cap/OD surface examination from the same probe position.
NDT QC
oral
Explain what 'back-scatter' is in radiography and how the letter 'B' on an RT film relates to it.

Grade on: Back-scatter — scattered radiation originating from behind the cassette (from walls, floor, tables behind the film) that strikes the back of the film, degrading image quality by adding fog; the letter 'B' (typically a lead letter) is placed on the back of the cassette during each exposure; if the letter 'B' appears as a light (less dark) image on the film, back-scatter is present and the film may be unacceptable; if 'B' is not visible on the film, back-scatter is not a significant problem for that exposure. The 'B' acts as a back-scatter indicator.
NDT QC
oral
A contractor tells you that they use TOFD for 100% weld examination and therefore do not need to perform any supplementary PT or MT. Is this correct? Explain.

Grade on: TOFD has inherent dead zones near both the OD surface (lateral wave dead zone) and ID surface (back wall dead zone), typically 2–5 mm from each surface depending on frequency and angle. Surface-connected defects within the dead zones may not be detected. Therefore, TOFD alone is not sufficient for full weld volume coverage — supplementary PT or MT (for surface defects) and possibly PAUT for near-surface zones are required to provide complete coverage per ASME VIII Div.1 Appendix 12 or relevant code.
NDT QC
oral
Why is it important to perform NDE AFTER PWHT for chromium-moly alloy welds, rather than before?

Grade on: PWHT changes the weld microstructure — it can: (1) reveal delayed hydrogen cracking that occurs after cooling (if any hydrogen is present); (2) cause reheat cracking in susceptible alloys (Cr-Mo steels) if PWHT parameters were incorrect; (3) expose pre-existing defects that grow due to thermal stress during PWHT; if NDE is done before PWHT, none of these post-PWHT defects would be detected. Final NDE after PWHT is the only valid method for certifying the as-delivered weld condition. This is a critical requirement in SAES-W-011.
NDT QC
oral
Explain what 'geometric unsharpness' (Ug) is in radiography and how reducing the source-to-film distance affects it.

Grade on: Geometric unsharpness (Ug) is the blurring (penumbra) at the edges of a radiographic image caused by the finite size of the radiation source; formula: Ug = f × d / SFD, where f = source focal spot size, d = object-to-film distance, SFD = source-to-film distance; reducing SFD (moving source closer) while keeping other parameters constant INCREASES Ug (more blurring) because there is less distance to reduce the penumbra effect; to maintain image quality while reducing SFD, either the source size must be reduced or the object-to-film distance must be reduced.

oral

You are conducting an NDT procedure review. The UT procedure states '45° refracted shear wave probe, scan from both sides.' The pipe has fillet welds on one side where the weld configuration physically prevents scanning from one side. What do you do?

Grade on: Physical access limitation means the 'scan from both sides' requirement cannot be met for these joints; this is a procedure deviation that must be formally documented; first, check whether the limited-access scanning from one side still provides adequate coverage (coverage analysis using beam spreading models); if adequate coverage can be demonstrated from one side using modified probe angles or positions, document this in a procedure supplement or deviation; if coverage is inadequate from one side, investigate supplementary NDE methods (RT, TOFD) or additional angles; never accept inadequate coverage without formal engineering evaluation.

During a walk-down you see the PT technician skipping the development stage and reading indications directly from the part after washing off the excess penetrant. What are the technical and procedural issues?

Grade on: Technical issue: without developer, the penetrant bleeds back from very fine discontinuities and creates an indication on the developer background — without developer, fine cracks are not reliably revealed; the developer provides a white contrasting background and draws penetrant out from cracks by capillary action; reading without developer completely defeats the purpose of the developer stage and will result in missed fine indications; procedural issue: developer application is a mandatory step per ASME V and the approved PT procedure — omitting it is a major nonconformance; all PT results from this session are invalid.
NDT QC
oral
What is the difference between 'calibration' and 'sensitivity setting' in ultrasonic testing?

Grade on: Calibration — setting the time base (distance calibration) so the screen displays the correct sound path distance using a reference block (V1/V2 block or IIW block); establishes that the A-scan reading of depth/distance is accurate. Sensitivity setting — adjusting the gain so that a specific reflector (SDH, notch, FBH) at a specific depth produces a specific screen amplitude (e.g., 80% FSH); this sets the examination sensitivity relative to the reference reflector. Calibration and sensitivity setting are separate steps; both must be performed and documented before examination begins.
NDT QC
oral

A production manager tells you that the project cannot afford 100% RT and wants to reduce to 10% random sampling. Your SAES-L-350 specification requires 100% RT for hydrogen service. How do you respond?

Grade on: The SAES-L-350 specification requirement for 100% RT in hydrogen service is not optional — it is a mandatory safety requirement based on the potential consequences of hydrogen embrittlement and cracking in H₂-containing lines; reducing NDE is a design/specification change that cannot be approved by the QC Inspector; escalate formally to the QC Manager and Project Manager; document the request and your response; a formal deviation request to ARAMCO Engineering would be required, and it is unlikely to be approved for hydrogen service; do not accept any verbal authorisation to reduce mandated NDE.
NDT QC
oral
Explain what 'inter-pass cleaning' means in welding and why it matters for RT acceptance of the final weld.

Grade on: Inter-pass cleaning — removal of slag, spatter, and oxide scale from each weld pass before the next pass is deposited; typically by chipping, grinding, and wire brushing; matters for RT because: inadequate cleaning leaves slag entrapped between passes — this shows as slag inclusions on the RT film, which may exceed acceptance criteria; slag between passes also acts as a barrier to fusion, potentially creating LOF defects; the NDT QC Inspector should verify inter-pass cleaning is being performed as part of in-process inspection.
NDT QC
oral
What is 'mode conversion' in ultrasonic testing and why is it particularly problematic when inspecting austenitic stainless steel welds?

Grade on: Mode conversion — when a shear wave (or longitudinal wave) strikes an interface at certain angles, part of the energy converts to the other mode (longitudinal ↔ shear); mode-converted waves travel at different velocities and arrive at different times, creating false indications or ghost signals that can be confused with real defects; in austenitic SS welds: the coarse, columnar grain structure is anisotropic (acoustic properties differ with direction), causing significant beam steering and mode conversion that produces high background noise (grain noise) that can mask real indications or generate numerous spurious signals; special low-frequency focused probes and PAUT with phased array are used to mitigate this.
NDT QC
oral

You find an RT film where the weld number is illegible — the lead number marker has fallen off the joint during exposure and the number is no longer readable. What are the implications and how do you resolve it?

Grade on: An RT film without a readable weld number cannot be traced to a specific joint — the film has no chain of custody to the weld it is supposed to represent; the film is invalid for acceptance purposes; the weld must be identified and re-radiographed with properly secured identification markers; if the weld cannot be physically identified, additional investigation (matching spool dimensional records, scanning sequence log) is required; issue a finding (NCR or corrective observation); corrective action: require technicians to secure lead markers with heat-resistant tape before exposure.
NDT QC
oral
Describe how you would prepare a punch list for final NDT record review before issuing a turnover package for a completed pressure piping system.

Grade on: Review every weld on the weld map against the NDT record; verify: (1) NDE report exists for each weld; (2) NDE report shows correct weld number, technique, date, technician name and certification, acceptance result; (3) Technique sheet and procedure revision in the report match the approved procedure; (4) IQI designation and sensitivity are correct for the weld thickness; (5) Film density readings recorded and within range; (6) Any rejected welds have NCR and subsequent acceptance after repair; (7) Technician certifications are current on the dates of examination; (8) No outstanding NCRs; list all discrepancies for corrective action before package issuance.
NDT QC
oral

A client's quality auditor tells you that the PT dwell time on your project has been 8 minutes when the procedure specifies 10 minutes. He wants to reject all welds examined in the past 2 weeks. Do you agree with this approach and what factors would you consider?

Grade on: The reduced dwell time is a procedural nonconformance that must be documented and investigated; however, blanket rejection of all welds without further assessment may be excessive; factors to consider: the difference (8 vs. 10 min) is 20% — is this within any stated tolerance in the procedure? Was the part temperature elevated (higher temperature slightly compensates by increasing penetrant mobility)? What types of defects was the PT intended to detect (surface cracks — penetrant dwell has more effect) vs. porosity (less dwell-time sensitive)? Recommended approach: NCR for all affected welds; enhanced re-examination by PT using correct 10-minute dwell; if no additional indications are found in the re-examination, the risk of missed indications from 2-minute shortfall is reassessed; complete rejection without re-examination is disproportionate.

practical

Review the following RT film interpretation record for a 12 mm thick CS butt weld (ASME B31.3 Normal Fluid Service) and identify any discrepancies: Film density: 2.8 H&D; IQI type: Wire (ASTM E747); IQI designation: 13 (diameter 0.406 mm); Required IQI per ASME V for 12 mm: 2-2T hole or equivalent wire; Indication: 4.5 mm rounded pore at weld centreline; Technician decision: ACCEPT.

Grade on: (1) Film density 2.8 — within 1.8–4.0 H&D range — OK; (2) Wire IQI No.13 (0.406 mm diameter) — verify against ASME V Table T-233.1 for 12 mm weld thickness; for 12 mm, the required essential wire is No.12 or 13 depending on the IQI type (verify); if No.13 is correct, OK; (3) 4.5 mm rounded pore in 12 mm weld — 1/4T = 3 mm, 6 mm maximum; 4.5 mm > 3 mm — REJECT per ASME B31.3 Table 341.3.2; Technician decision 'ACCEPT' is WRONG. The film must be rejected and the weld repaired. Issue NCR.
