practical

A UT calibration record for an angle beam 45° examination shows the following V-path calibration data: Screen position 2 = 100 mm (1/2 skip); Screen position 4 = 200 mm (full skip). The actual part wall thickness is 25 mm. Calculate the expected screen positions (in mm of sound path) for a reflector at: (a) 10 mm depth from OD; (b) 25 mm depth (ID surface/root).

Grade on: For 45° refracted shear wave: sound path = depth / cos(45°) = depth × 1.414; (a) 10 mm depth from OD — sound path = 10 / cos(45°) = 10 × 1.414 = 14.1 mm (first leg); screen should show approximately 14 mm; (b) 25 mm depth (ID, half-skip) — sound path = 25 / cos(45°) = 35.4 mm; screen position ≈ 35 mm at half-skip position. Note: this is a simplified calculation — actual UT calibration uses the V-path directly on the calibration block, so the screen positions should match the physical half-skip geometry (25 mm × 2 / tan(45°) = 50 mm actual half-skip distance from probe index).
NDT QC
practical

You receive a completed holiday test (HT) report for a shop-coated 20-inch OD CS pipe with 3LPE coating, nominal DFT 3 mm. The report states: Test voltage 5,000 V; 3 holidays found at joints 4, 7, and 12; joints repaired and re-tested; 0 holidays after repair. Identify whether the test voltage is appropriate and state your finding on the overall HT report.

Grade on: NACE SP0188 test voltage for 3 mm 3LPE coating — formula: 100 V per mil = 100 × 120 mils (3 mm = 120 mils) = 12,000 V or use 4 V/μm × 3000 μm = 12,000 V; the report states 5,000 V — this is significantly below the required ~12,000 V; at 5,000 V, the test will miss many holidays in a 3 mm coating because the voltage is insufficient to arc through the full coating thickness to contact the steel; finding: the holiday test was performed at incorrect voltage; all pipe joints must be re-tested at the correct voltage (~12,000 V) before acceptance; previously reported 'repair and re-test' results are also invalid.
NDT QC
practical

Review a PAUT scan display (B-scan, top view) showing an indication that starts at 3 mm depth from OD, grows to 8 mm depth, and continues for 35 mm along the weld length. The wall thickness is 20 mm. The rejection criterion for ASME VIII Div.2 Chapter 7 for planar indications is: length >25 mm or through-wall height >3 mm (whichever is more restrictive). Evaluate this indication.

Grade on: Length: 35 mm > 25 mm maximum — FAIL on length criterion; Through-wall height: the indication spans 3–8 mm depth = 5 mm through-wall height; 5 mm > 3 mm maximum — FAIL on height criterion. The indication fails both criteria independently. Finding: REJECT — two independent rejection criteria are exceeded. This is a significant planar defect (likely LOF or crack type) that must be excavated, repaired, and re-examined.
NDT QC
practical

A PT report of a pressure vessel nozzle weld shows the following: Penetrant type: Zyglo ZL-67 (fluorescent, Type I); Developer: ZP-9B (non-aqueous wet); UV-A light intensity: 1,050 μW/cm² measured at the inspection surface; Ambient visible light: 120 lux; Dwell time: 10 minutes at 22°C surface temperature; Evaluation: No relevant indications. Confirm whether each parameter is compliant with ASME V Article 6.

Grade on: (1) Penetrant Type I fluorescent — acceptable; (2) Non-aqueous wet developer — acceptable for Type I fluorescent; (3) UV-A intensity 1,050 μW/cm² — ASME V T-676.1 requires ≥1000 μW/cm² — PASS; (4) Ambient light 120 lux — ASME V T-676.1 requires ≤20 lux ambient for fluorescent evaluation — 120 lux FAILS — examination is invalid; (5) Dwell time 10 min at 22°C — within acceptable range — PASS. Primary nonconformance: ambient visible light 120 lux far exceeds the 20 lux maximum for fluorescent PT. Examination must be repeated in compliant lighting conditions.
NDT QC
practical

Calculate the Geometric Unsharpness (Ug) for the following RT exposure parameters and determine whether it meets ASME V requirements (Ug ≤ 0.51 mm): Source: Ir-192, focal spot size = 2.5 mm; Source-to-film distance (SFD) = 800 mm; Film-to-object distance (d) = 10 mm (film directly on pipe OD, pipe wall = 10 mm from ID).

Grade on: Formula: Ug = f × d / (SFD − d) ≈ f × d / SFD for small d relative to SFD; Ug = 2.5 × 10 / 800 = 0.031 mm. Wait — more correctly: Ug = f × d / (SFD − d) = 2.5 × 10 / (800 − 10) = 25 / 790 = 0.032 mm. 0.032 mm < 0.51 mm maximum — PASS. Note: the calculation shows Ug is well within the acceptable limit for this SFD and source size. Candidate must know the formula and apply it correctly.
NDT QC
practical

Review the following MT (MPI) examination setup data and identify all nonconformances per ASME V Article 7: AC yoke; Lift test performed at start of shift (4.5 kg — pass); Magnetisation direction: single direction (longitudinal, parallel to weld axis) only; Wet fluorescent particles; UV-A light at 900 μW/cm² at inspection surface; Evaluation: 2 indications found, both less than 3 mm — ACCEPTED per D1.1.

Grade on: (1) Single magnetisation direction only — FAIL — ASME V T-750 requires magnetisation in two directions at approximately 90° to each other to detect defects in all orientations; single direction (parallel to weld axis) detects only transverse defects — longitudinal defects (most common weld defects) will be missed; (2) UV-A intensity 900 μW/cm² — ASME V T-753 requires ≥1000 μW/cm² — FAIL; (3) Lift test result of 4.5 kg for AC yoke — ASME V T-750.2 AC yoke ≥4.5 kg — PASS; (4) Wet fluorescent particles — acceptable method. Two nonconformances: single magnetisation direction and sub-standard UV intensity.
NDT QC
practical

An RT exposure record shows the following for a 10-inch, 12.7 mm wall pipe weld SWSI (Single Wall Single Image) technique: SFD = 900 mm; Film: Agfa D7; Source: Se-75, 40 Ci; Exposure time: 45 minutes; IQI: Wire No.12 source side; Film density measured: 3.6 H&D; Technician: Level II, certification expires in 6 months. Verify each parameter and state the overall film acceptance.

Grade on: (1) SFD 900 mm — calculate Ug: Se-75 focal spot ≈ 1.5–2 mm; Ug = 2 × 12.7 / 900 ≈ 0.028 mm — well within 0.51 mm limit; (2) Film density 3.6 — within 1.8–4.0 H&D range — PASS; (3) Wire IQI No.12 (source side) — verify against ASME V Table T-233.1 for 12.7 mm; check if No.12 (0.356 mm) is the correct required essential wire for this wall thickness (typically acceptable); (4) Se-75 isotope — appropriate for thin-to-medium thickness pipe; (5) Technician certification valid for 6 more months — PASS; (6) Exposure time 45 min — verify against exposure chart but cannot evaluate without more data; accept as field-determined. Overall: the visible parameters are within acceptable limits — film should be reviewed for indication content.
NDT QC
practical

You are reviewing a PAUT calibration certificate for a phased array probe used on a 25 mm wall CS weld examination. The calibration data shows: Probe: 5 MHz, 16-element linear array; Reference block: CS, 25 mm thickness, with SDH 2 mm diameter at 1/4T, 1/2T, 3/4T depths; DAC curve reference points: 1/4T = 78% FSH, 1/2T = 80% FSH (reference), 3/4T = 65% FSH. The examination procedure requires the DAC to be set from the 1/2T SDH. Evaluate the calibration data.

Grade on: The DAC curve should show decreasing amplitude with increasing depth due to beam spreading and attenuation. However, 1/4T (78%) is lower than 1/2T (80%), which is unusual — the near-surface reflector should show higher amplitude than mid-depth due to less path length attenuation. This inversion (78% at 1/4T vs. 80% at 1/2T) suggests near-surface dead zone effects, near-field probe effects, or probe-to-surface coupling variation at the short path. The calibration should be investigated — the technician should verify coupling conditions at the 1/4T SDH and confirm whether a gain transfer correction is needed for the near-surface zone. An anomalous DAC curve is a calibration quality concern.
NDT QC
practical

A weld map shows 45 girth welds. The NDE log shows 40 RT reports filed. Check whether the 10% random RT requirement of ASME B31.3 for Normal Fluid Service is met, and determine whether the correct sample was tested assuming design requires 10% random RT of girth welds.

Grade on: 10% of 45 welds = 4.5 → minimum 5 welds required (round up per ASME B31.3 para 341.3.4); 40 reports filed — this is 89% coverage, which far exceeds the 10% minimum. If 40 of 45 welds were RT'd, that is excessive relative to the specification (but not a violation — more NDE is conservative). The candidate should note: (1) 40/45 = 89% examined — more than required; (2) 5 welds have no RT report — are these in the 90% not required? Yes, 5 of 45 = 11% unexamined, which is within the allowance for 10% random examination. The NDE programme is ACCEPTABLE — but the inspector should verify that the 5 unexamined welds were not selected for mandatory inspection by any criterion (e.g., selected based on risk — if any were selected, they must be examined).
NDT QC
practical

Evaluate the following UT indication disposition for a 20 mm wall pressure pipe (ASME B31.3 para 341.3.3): Indication: amplitude 100% DAC (at rejection level); Location: 5 mm below OD surface (upper 1/4T zone); Length: 20 mm; Through-wall height (from -6 dB drop sizing): 3 mm. Acceptance criteria: reject any planar indication where through-wall height >1/4T or >6 mm (whichever less).

Grade on: 1/4T = 20/4 = 5 mm; lesser of 5 mm and 6 mm = 5 mm maximum through-wall height allowed. Measured through-wall height = 3 mm < 5 mm — within height limit. However: amplitude at 100% DAC meets the amplitude rejection threshold defined in the procedure. Check: does the procedure reject at 100% DAC regardless of size, or use DAC only as a recording/characterisation threshold with size-based final acceptance? If the procedure uses DAC as the rejection level (signal ≥ DAC = reject), the indication is REJECTED. If DAC is the recording threshold and size governs final acceptance, then the 3 mm through-wall height may be acceptable. The candidate must recognise this ambiguity and request clarification of the procedure acceptance criteria. This is the most common field dispute in UT acceptance.
NDT QC
practical

Review the following PT indication record and state your acceptance decision per ASME VIII Div.1 Appendix 8: Indication No.1: Linear, 4 mm long at weld toe; Indication No.2: Round, 1.2 mm diameter at weld cap centreline; Indication No.3: Linear, 1.2 mm long at weld HAZ (categorised as 'arc strike' by technician); Indication No.4: Round, 0.4 mm diameter (technician categorises as 'penetrant entrapment in surface scratch').

Grade on: ASME VIII Div.1 Appendix 8 acceptance: all linear indications ≥1.5 mm are rejectable; rounded indications: ≥5 mm rejected; if four or more in a line separated by <1.5 mm aggregate = 13 mm rejected. Indication 1: 4 mm linear — REJECT (4 mm ≥ 1.5 mm); Indication 2: 1.2 mm round — ACCEPT (< 5 mm); Indication 3: 1.2 mm linear (arc strike) — REJECT (1.2 mm ≥ 1.5 mm? — 1.2 mm < 1.5 mm — borderline ACCEPT on PT criteria, but arc strike is a separate NCR issue regardless); Indication 4: 0.4 mm round — technician calls it false — if confirmed false indication (re-PT shows no indication): ACCEPT. Summary: Indication 1 REJECT; Indications 2 and 4 ACCEPT (if confirmed); Indication 3 requires arc strike NCR separate from PT acceptance.
NDT QC
practical

A Guided Wave (LRUT) screening survey of a 6-inch insulated CS pipe indicates a reflector at 14 metres distance with -15 dB amplitude relative to the weld reference. The survey report states 'possible corrosion — investigate.' You review the report. What minimum follow-up NDE is required and how would you prioritise inspection at the reflector location?

Grade on: Guided wave LRUT is a screening tool — it identifies locations for further investigation, not a final acceptance/rejection method; for a -15 dB reflector (potentially significant metal loss): prioritise the location for direct-access inspection; remove insulation at 14 m ± 0.5 m; perform point UTT measurements on a grid pattern (minimum 6 points around circumference at the indicated position); if UTT shows thickness below minimum required, expand mapping (C-scan UT or profile RT); assess findings against API 570 minimum remaining thickness; if the location cannot be physically accessed (buried, elevated), use an alternative such as UT crawler or drain-down and direct inspection.
NDT QC
practical

An eddy current examination of heat exchanger tubes shows the following indications for Tube A (OD 25 mm, wall 2.5 mm, admiralty brass): Signal 1: amplitude 75% of calibration, phase angle 35°; Signal 2: amplitude 20%, phase angle 85°. Using standard ECT lissajous interpretation for admiralty brass tube examination (OD surface defects: low phase angle 20–40°; ID surface defects: high phase angle 70–90°), characterise each signal and state whether either requires tube plugging or repair.

Grade on: Signal 1: 75% amplitude, 35° phase — consistent with OD (outer surface) volumetric defect; 75% amplitude relative to calibration notch suggests significant wall loss; if the calibration notch is 20% wall loss, estimate the actual depth using the amplitude-to-depth curve from the calibration standard; a 75% signal typically represents >40–50% wall loss depending on calibration — this would likely trigger plugging if it represents >50% wall loss; Signal 2: 20% amplitude, 85° phase — consistent with ID (inner surface) defect; 20% amplitude is small, likely minor pitting; may not require immediate action but should be monitored. Candidate should state that the calibration curve must be applied to convert amplitude to percent wall loss before a final recommendation on plugging.
NDT QC
practical

You are reviewing a TOFD D-scan for a 50 mm pressure vessel seam weld. The scan shows: lateral wave at T=0.25 μs; back wall at T=2.15 μs; an indication at T=1.8 μs spanning 40 mm along the weld. Calculate the approximate depth of the indication from the OD surface using the acoustic velocity in steel of 5,900 m/s (longitudinal wave).

Grade on: TOFD depth calculation: time for lateral wave (t_L) = 0.25 μs; time for back wall (t_BW) = 2.15 μs; total transit time for 50 mm = t_BW − t_L = 2.15 − 0.25 = 1.90 μs for 100 mm round trip (50 mm depth × 2); time ratio for indication: t_ind − t_L = 1.80 − 0.25 = 1.55 μs; depth = (1.55 / 1.90) × 50 mm = 40.8 mm from OD surface. Indication is approximately 41 mm depth — this is in the near-ID zone (50 − 41 = 9 mm from ID surface); this may be within the back wall dead zone — supplementary PAUT may be needed for reliable sizing. The 40 mm length of the indication and its near-ID position makes this a significant finding requiring further investigation.
NDT QC
practical

Review the following RT report data for a 19 mm thick pressure vessel seam weld and identify any issues before signing the report: Date: 2025-10-01; Weld ID: V-22-03; Technique: SWSI; Source: Ir-192, 45 Ci; SFD: 700 mm; Film: Agfa D7; IQI: Wire No.16 (1.0 mm diameter) source side; Film density: 2.5 H&D; Coverage: 100% (12 films, 150 mm each); Indication: 3 mm isolated pore; Technician Level II certification: CSWIP PCN RT Level 2, expires 2026-05-15; Acceptance per ASME VIII Div.1: ACCEPT.

Grade on: (1) IQI Wire No.16 (1.0 mm): check ASME V Table T-233.1 for 19 mm — required essential wire is typically No.13 (0.406 mm) for this thickness; Wire No.16 (1.0 mm) is a thicker wire and represents LESS sensitive IQI than required — the procedure requires the essential wire to be visible, and if a thicker (less sensitive) wire is used, the required sensitivity level is not confirmed; this is a FAIL; (2) 3 mm isolated pore in 19 mm wall: 1/4T = 4.75 mm; 3 mm < 4.75 mm AND < 6 mm — ASME VIII porosity chart must be applied but 3 mm isolated pore in 19 mm wall is likely ACCEPTABLE; (3) Certification: current to 2026-05 — PASS. Primary issue: IQI designation may be incorrect — verify No.16 vs. required essential wire for 19 mm.
NDT QC
practical

A weld inspection record shows that UT angle-beam examination was completed on Weld W-45 (16 mm wall, ASME B31.3 Category M toxic service) using a 45° probe only. The approved procedure requires examination with both 45° and 60° probes for this wall thickness to ensure full weld volume coverage. Evaluate the nonconformance and state what additional action is required.

Grade on: Single-angle examination (45° only) on a 16 mm wall weld is likely inadequate for full coverage — the 60° probe covers different angular zones and is particularly important for detecting planar defects (LOF) at different orientations in the weld; ASME B31.3 Category M toxic service requires 100% RT or volumetric examination — UT with incomplete coverage is a nonconformance; required additional action: re-examine all W-45 weld volume with 60° probe and document the results; any indications found during the 60° scan that were missed by the 45° scan must be dispositioned per the applicable acceptance criteria; issue NCR for incomplete examination.
NDT QC
practical

Evaluate the following MT examination setup for a CS structural weld using the prod technique: Prod spacing: 150 mm; Current: 450 A AC; Magnetic field adequacy indicator (pie gauge): not used; Prod burns: 3 burns visible on the base metal adjacent to the weld; Indication: No indications found — ACCEPT.

Grade on: (1) Prod spacing 150 mm — within typical range (75–200 mm); (2) Current 450 A AC — verify against ASME V T-756 (typically 300–800 A for 100–200 mm spacing — within range); (3) Pie gauge not used — ASME V T-750.1 does not mandate pie gauge use but it is used to verify field direction; while not a code violation, its absence means field direction coverage was not independently verified; (4) Prod burns — prod burns (arc burns) on the base metal are a SIGNIFICANT NONCONFORMANCE; they are hard spots (untempered martensite) that must be ground out, PT'd, and the area verified to be defect-free; they are also a procedural violation (ASME V T-756.1: prods shall not be held in one position while current is flowing); finding: prod burns are rejectable — NCR required.
NDT QC
practical

Review the following UT amplitude correction calculation: Calibration was performed at 25°C. The UT instrument's temperature compensation curve shows a 1.5 dB change per 10°C temperature variation. During examination, the pipe temperature was 60°C. What temperature correction should be applied to the calibration amplitude, and in which direction?

Grade on: Temperature change = 60 − 25 = 35°C. Correction = 35/10 × 1.5 dB = 5.25 dB. Direction: higher temperature increases attenuation in the material (particularly in carbon steel) — the probe coupling may also be affected; the gain should be INCREASED by approximately 5.25 dB to compensate for the higher attenuation at 60°C relative to the 25°C calibration. Alternatively, the technician should re-calibrate at the actual examination temperature (preferred practice). Note: specific temperature compensation must follow the instrument manufacturer's calibration procedure and material-specific curves.
NDT QC
practical

You receive the following summary of NDT examination results for a completed 50-weld piping spool (ASME B31.3 Category M, 100% RT required): RT complete: 47 welds; RT pending: 3 welds (W-28, W-41, W-47); Accepted: 44 welds; Rejected: 3 welds (W-12 repaired and re-RT accepted, W-33 repaired pending re-RT, W-38 outstanding NCR). The spool is being pressured for hydrostatic testing. Evaluate whether the spool is ready for pressure testing.

Grade on: NOT READY for hydrotest. Issues: (1) RT pending for W-28, W-41, W-47 — 100% RT requirement means no untested welds; pressure test cannot proceed; (2) W-33: repaired but re-RT pending — unaccepted weld; cannot proceed; (3) W-38: outstanding NCR — must be closed/dispositioned before hydrotest; Ready welds: 44 (accepted) + W-12 (repaired and accepted) = 45. Remaining: 3 pending RT + 1 pending re-RT + 1 outstanding NCR = 5 items must be resolved. Minimum actions before hydrotest: complete RT on W-28, W-41, W-47; complete re-RT on W-33; close NCR on W-38 with accepted disposition.
Mechanical QC
mcq

A pressure vessel nameplate shows MAWP 50 bar at 300°C and MWP at new and cold condition of 65 bar. A maintenance team proposes to hydrotest the vessel at 1.5 × 65 bar = 97.5 bar. What is the correct hydrotest pressure?

97.5 bar — the hydrostatic test pressure per ASME VIII UG-99 is 1.5 × MAWP-new-and-cold.
75 bar — the hydrostatic test pressure per ASME VIII UG-99(b) is 1.3 × MAWP at the design temperature, corrected by the stress ratio for ambient temperature.
75 bar — the hydrostatic test pressure is 1.5 × MAWP at design temperature.
97.5 bar — ASME VIII allows any multiplier above 1.5 × MAWP at the inspector's discretion.
75 bar — the hydrostatic test pressure per ASME VIII UG-99(b) is 1.3 × MAWP at the design temperature, corrected by the stress ratio for ambient temperature.

ASME VIII Div.1 UG-99(b): minimum hydrostatic test pressure = 1.3 × MAWP × (allowable stress at test temperature / allowable stress at design temperature). Using MAWP at design temperature (50 bar): 1.3 × 50 = 65 bar minimum (before stress ratio correction). Using MAWP new-and-cold (65 bar): 1.3 × 65 = 84.5 bar minimum. Many candidates confuse the 1.5× multiplier (old edition) with the current 1.3× per ASME VIII-1 2017+.
Mechanical QC
mcq

During a pressure vessel external inspection per API 510, the inspector discovers corrosion on the shell with minimum measured thickness of 8.5 mm. The minimum required thickness calculated by the original design is 7.2 mm. The original nominal shell plate thickness was 12 mm. What is the corrosion allowance remaining?

4.5 mm remaining (nominal 12 mm minus 7.2 mm minimum)
1.3 mm remaining (measured 8.5 mm minus minimum required 7.2 mm)
3.5 mm remaining (measured 8.5 mm minus minimum required 5.0 mm using half the design CA)
0 mm remaining — the vessel is at minimum acceptable thickness and must be repaired.
1.3 mm remaining (measured 8.5 mm minus minimum required 7.2 mm)

Remaining corrosion allowance = actual measured thickness − minimum required thickness = 8.5 − 7.2 = 1.3 mm. This represents what can be lost before the vessel falls below the code minimum. Distractor A calculates total original corrosion allowance (12 − 7.2 = 4.8 mm) but this is not the remaining allowance.
Mechanical QC
mcq

A centrifugal pump alignment report shows the following cold alignment readings (dial gauge method): Angular misalignment: 0.08 mm/100 mm (spec ≤ 0.05 mm/100 mm); Parallel misalignment: 0.03 mm (spec ≤ 0.05 mm). The operator wants to run the pump at ambient temperature before performing hot alignment checks. What is the correct finding?

Acceptable — parallel alignment within spec, start the pump and verify hot alignment later.
Not acceptable — angular misalignment of 0.08 mm/100 mm exceeds the 0.05 mm/100 mm specification, the pump cannot be started until cold alignment is within all specifications.
Acceptable — angular misalignment is within the 0.10 mm/100 mm general tolerance for centrifugal pumps per API 686.
Not acceptable — both angular and parallel misalignment readings must be zero before starting any rotating equipment.
Not acceptable — angular misalignment of 0.08 mm/100 mm exceeds the 0.05 mm/100 mm specification, the pump cannot be started until cold alignment is within all specifications.

Both alignment parameters must meet specification before start-up. Angular misalignment of 0.08 mm/100 mm exceeds the 0.05 mm/100 mm limit by 60%. Running with excessive angular misalignment causes accelerated bearing wear, coupling failure, and seal damage. Cold alignment must meet all specs; hot alignment check is performed additionally, not instead of cold alignment compliance.
Mechanical QC
mcq

A pressure relief valve (PRV) has a set pressure of 100 bar. During a bench test per API 527, the PRV opens at 104 bar and reseats at 91 bar. The blowdown is therefore 13%. ASME VIII allows a maximum blowdown of 7% of set pressure (7 bar maximum). What is the finding?

Accept — the opening at 104 bar is within the +3% lift tolerance per API 527.
Reject — the 13% blowdown (104 − 91 = 13 bar) exceeds the 7% maximum (7 bar), the PRV must be returned to the manufacturer for re-adjustment and re-testing.
Accept — a 13% blowdown is within the typical 10–15% allowed for balanced bellows PRVs.
Accept — the reseat pressure of 91 bar is above 88 bar (12% below set) which is the absolute minimum.
Reject — the 13% blowdown (104 − 91 = 13 bar) exceeds the 7% maximum (7 bar), the PRV must be returned to the manufacturer for re-adjustment and re-testing.

Blowdown = (set pressure − reseat pressure) / set pressure = (104 − 91) / 100 = 13%. ASME VIII UG-134: maximum allowable blowdown is 7% of set pressure for most vapour service PRVs. 13% > 7% maximum — the PRV fails the bench test and must be adjusted. Opening at 104 bar is within the +3% tolerance separately.
Mechanical QC
mcq

A pressure vessel inspection reveals weld overlay cladding (Alloy 825) on the inside surface of a CS vessel shell. The overlay is applied in two layers. During UT thickness measurement, the technician measures 42 mm total (including cladding). The overlay design thickness is 5 mm. The CS shell minimum required thickness is 35 mm. Is the shell acceptable?

Yes — total thickness 42 mm minus cladding 5 mm = 37 mm CS, 37 mm > 35 mm minimum — acceptable.
No — the total thickness including cladding must equal at least 40 mm, 42 mm − 5 mm = 37 mm is below the required 40 mm combined thickness.
Yes — total thickness 42 mm exceeds the minimum required thickness of 35 mm.
No — weld overlay cladding cannot be counted as structural shell thickness per ASME VIII Div.1.
Yes — total thickness 42 mm minus cladding 5 mm = 37 mm CS, 37 mm > 35 mm minimum — acceptable.

In pressure vessel FFS assessment: the cladding overlay (corrosion-resistant, non-structural) is typically not counted toward the structural minimum thickness. CS structural thickness = total − cladding = 42 − 5 = 37 mm. 37 mm > 35 mm minimum required → acceptable. Distractor C incorrectly counts total thickness including cladding as structural.
Mechanical QC
mcq

During a mechanical installation inspection of a gearbox, the inspector finds that the oil sump temperature is reaching 95°C during initial no-load run-in. The equipment data sheet specifies a maximum operating oil temperature of 80°C. What is the correct action?

Accept — oil temperature typically stabilises after the initial run-in period, allow another 2 hours of operation.
Stop the equipment — the oil temperature exceeds the 80°C maximum, investigate the cause (insufficient cooling, incorrect oil grade, blocked oil passages, misalignment) before resuming operation.
Accept — a 15°C overrun is within the typical ±20°C tolerance for gearbox oil temperature during run-in.
Reduce load on the gearbox to 50% until the oil temperature stabilises within specification.
Stop the equipment — the oil temperature exceeds the 80°C maximum, investigate the cause (insufficient cooling, incorrect oil grade, blocked oil passages, misalignment) before resuming operation.

Equipment must operate within specified parameters during run-in testing. A 95°C oil temperature in a gearbox specified for 80°C maximum could cause accelerated oil degradation, seal damage, and bearing failure. Root cause investigation is required before resuming operation. 'Wait and see' approaches on rotating equipment are not acceptable QC practice.
Mechanical QC
mcq

An API 650 above-ground storage tank inspection reveals a shell plate with a measured thickness of 4.2 mm. The minimum allowable thickness per API 653 for this shell course (corroded allowance excluded) is 5.0 mm. The remaining life based on the corrosion rate is 2 years. What is the assessment?

Accept — the 2-year remaining life exceeds the typical 1-year inspection interval.
The shell course is below minimum thickness — the tank must be removed from service, repaired or replaced, or a formal FFS assessment per API 653 Section 9 performed before any continued operation.
Accept — 4.2 mm is within the 20% tolerance below minimum thickness allowed by API 653.
Accept with a monitored inspection programme every 6 months.
The shell course is below minimum thickness — the tank must be removed from service, repaired or replaced, or a formal FFS assessment per API 653 Section 9 performed before any continued operation.

API 653 para 4.4: if measured thickness is below the calculated minimum, the shell is unacceptable for continued operation at the current conditions. A formal API 579 FFS or API 653 Section 9 assessment is required. Simply monitoring does not address the current below-minimum thickness finding.
Mechanical QC
mcq

During pre-commissioning inspection of a shell-and-tube heat exchanger, the inspector finds that the tube-to-tubesheet joint drawing specifies expanded AND welded joints (explosive expansion + TIG seal weld). The fabrication records show only expanded joints were made — no welding was performed. What is the finding?

Accept — tube expansion alone provides sufficient sealing for most heat exchanger service conditions.
Major NCR — the fabrication deviated from the specified joint design, expanded-only joints may not meet the design pressure or leak-tightness requirements for the service, the tubesheet welds must be performed or a formal concession obtained from the design engineer.
Accept — seal welding is an optional step in TEMA standards for moderate pressure applications.
Accept — the tube expansion can be verified by helium leak testing, if no leaks are found, welding is not required.

Major NCR — the fabrication deviated from the specified joint design, expanded-only joints may not meet the design pressure or leak-tightness requirements for the service, the tubesheet welds must be performed or a formal concession obtained from the design engineer.

The design engineer specified an expanded-AND-welded joint for a reason (higher design pressure, toxic service, or cyclic service requiring full strength joint). Deviation from the specified joint type is a fabrication nonconformance that must be dispositioned formally. Expansion-only joints have lower strength and leak resistance than welded joints — a helium leak test alone is not sufficient to confirm strength equivalence.
Mechanical QC
mcq

A rotating equipment foundation alignment check shows that the pump baseplate has been installed with a 3 mm low spot at one corner. Specification requires the baseplate to be level within ±1.5 mm over its full length. Grouting is already complete and cured. What is the finding?

Accept — a 3 mm difference over a large baseplate represents a very small angle and will not affect alignment.
NCR — the baseplate levelness of 3 mm out-of-specification cannot be corrected after grouting without major rework, the grout must be removed, the baseplate re-levelled and re-grouted.
Accept — correct the offset by re-shimming the equipment feet during the final alignment procedure.
Accept — the 3 mm deviation is within the ±3 mm typical tolerance for equipment bases.
NCR — the baseplate levelness of 3 mm out-of-specification cannot be corrected after grouting without major rework, the grout must be removed, the baseplate re-levelled and re-grouted.

Baseplate levelness directly affects the long-term ability to maintain equipment alignment and shaft loads. A 3 mm low spot (double the ±1.5 mm specification) is a significant deviation that will cause unequal load distribution and make precise alignment difficult. Once grouted, re-levelling requires removing the grout — the correct action is NCR and rework.

Above 10%, the spring-loaded conventional design either has reduced lift (doesn't open fully) or chatters. Balanced bellows PRVs can tolerate up to 50% back pressure. The corrective action is design modification.

Without looking at an API standard, explain what the 'Nelson Curve' is and why it matters for pressure vessel inspection in a hydrogen plant.

Grade on: The Nelson Curve (API RP 941, Steels for Hydrogen Service at Elevated Temperatures and Pressures) defines the safe operating envelope for carbon and low-alloy steels in H₂-H₂S service — it plots temperature vs. hydrogen partial pressure; above the curve for a given material, high-temperature hydrogen attack (HTHA) occurs — hydrogen reacts with carbides, causing decarburisation, methane bubble formation, and eventual embrittlement or fissuring; matters for inspection because: a vessel operating near or above the Nelson Curve for its material grade requires urgent upgrade to Mo-containing steel or reduction in operating conditions; failure to recognise HTHA risk has caused catastrophic vessel failures.

Explain what 'settling' of a tank foundation means and why it matters for storage tank integrity.

Grade on: Settling — differential or uniform downward movement of a storage tank foundation due to soil consolidation, loading, or soil erosion; differential settling (uneven) is the more dangerous form — it causes the tank shell to deform from circular to elliptical, creating bending stresses in the shell-to-bottom annular plate weld; if differential settlement exceeds API 653 criteria (typically >0.3% of tank diameter as maximum differential between diametrically opposite points for uniform settlement, or local settlement exceeding shell bending limit), the tank requires inspection and potentially remediation (soil stabilisation, re-levelling); API 653 Appendix B provides settlement monitoring criteria and evaluation methods.
Mechanical QC

The production team wants to bypass the low-pressure alarm on a pressure vessel to 'avoid nuisance trips.' How do you respond?

Grade on: Instrumented protection system (low-pressure alarm/trip) on a pressure vessel exists for a safety reason — typically to detect a leak or process upset and protect personnel and equipment; bypassing it requires a formal Management of Change (MOC) process including safety review (HAZOP/LOPA); the bypass cannot be done casually — even a temporary bypass must be formally approved, logged, and time-limited with compensating measures; as QC Inspector, document the request and request formal MOC documentation; do not approve or endorse any safety system bypass without formal MOC clearance; escalate to the project QC Manager and HSE team.

Explain what 'NPSH' (Net Positive Suction Head) is and why it is critical for centrifugal pump commissioning.

Grade on: NPSH — Net Positive Suction Head; NPSHa (available) is the total head at the pump suction minus the vapour pressure of the fluid; NPSHr (required) is the minimum head at the pump inlet (by the pump manufacturer) to prevent cavitation; cavitation occurs when NPSHa < NPSHr — liquid flashes to vapour at the impeller eye, creating bubbles that collapse violently, eroding the impeller and causing vibration; commissioning relevance: must verify NPSHa > NPSHr + 0.5 m safety margin at the design flow rate; check: suction pipe size (resistance reduces NPSHa), fluid temperature (higher temp raises vapour pressure, reducing NPSHa), tank liquid level (lower level reduces NPSHa); symptoms of cavitation: noisy operation, vibration, erosion of impeller.
Mechanical QC
oral
You are reviewing a fabrication traveller and notice that the pressure test was performed before the PWHT for an ASME VIII vessel in sour service. Explain the implication.

Grade on: A pressure test conducted before PWHT is invalid for the final acceptance of the vessel — PWHT changes the weld microstructure and residual stress state; if PWHT reveals or causes cracks (reheat cracking, hydrogen-induced cracking from the test water), those defects would exist in the final vessel but were not detected; the pressure test must be performed AFTER all PWHT has been completed to test the final material condition; additionally, for sour service vessels, PWHT is required to achieve the NACE hardness limits — if the vessel is tested before PWHT, it has not yet been treated to meet sour service requirements; the test must be repeated after PWHT.

oral
What is 'corrosion under insulation' (CUI) and name three types of equipment that are most vulnerable to it.

Grade on: CUI — corrosion that occurs beneath thermal insulation due to trapped moisture; the insulation keeps moisture in contact with the metal surface for extended periods; most vulnerable equipment: (1) process piping with insulation that has damaged or breached weatherproofing (Al jacketing); (2) pressure vessel nozzles where insulation terminates or is thin (especially at support shoe contacts); (3) heat exchanger shells with intermittent insulation; (4) carbon steel equipment operating at temperatures between −4°C and 175°C (highest CUI risk range); risk factors: proximity to water sources (cooling towers, wash-down areas), high humidity environments (Middle East coastal), and intermittent operation (wet/dry cycling).

A pressure vessel owner wants to operate a vessel rated for 100 bar at 250°C at a higher temperature of 280°C. He says the pressure will remain at 100 bar. What is the technical concern?

Grade on: Pressure vessel allowable stress reduces with increasing temperature — ASME VIII Div.1 allowable stresses are temperature-dependent (per ASME II Part D); at 280°C, the allowable stress for the vessel material is lower than at 250°C; if the vessel was designed exactly to minimum required thickness at 250°C, operating at 280°C at the same pressure may exceed the allowable stress; the actual MAWP at 280°C is lower than 100 bar; additionally, higher temperature may affect the corrosion rate and remaining life assessment; a formal re-rating assessment per API 510 is required at the new temperature before any change in operating conditions.

You are inspecting a fired heater and notice that one tube appears to have a slight bulge near the top of the radiant section. The operator says it's been there for 6 months and hasn't changed. What do you do?

Grade on: A bulge on a fired heater tube is an extremely serious finding — it indicates creep deformation from overheating (flame impingement, flame failure resulting in hot spot, maldistribution of flow, fouling) or corrosion creating a thin spot that bulges under internal pressure; immediate action: shut down the heater or at minimum the affected pass — a bulging tube is a pre-failure condition that can rupture catastrophically into the firebox; the tube cannot remain in service until the bulge is evaluated (UT to determine wall thickness at the bulge, metallurgical analysis of a sample if possible); 'unchanged for 6 months' does not mean safe — creep is a cumulative, temperature-dependent process and the bulge could rupture without further growth warning.

Describe three key differences between an ASME VIII Div.1 and Div.2 pressure vessel from an inspection perspective.

Grade on: (1) Div.1 uses a simpler, more conservative design approach (lower maximum allowable stress = thicker walls); Div.2 allows higher stresses (thinner walls) but requires more rigorous analysis (detailed stress analysis, fatigue assessment) — this means Div.2 vessels require higher-quality NDE and documentation during fabrication; (2) NDE requirements: Div.1 allows partial RT with joint efficiency factor; Div.2 requires 100% volumetric NDE (RT or UT) on all pressure welds; (3) Div.2 requires impact testing in more cases (for all materials below a certain temperature threshold) than Div.1; for inspectors, a Div.2 vessel has a more complete fabrication and inspection records package and typically requires tighter dimensional and NDE acceptance criteria.

A maintenance engineer proposes to repair an internal crack in a pressure vessel shell by grinding the crack out and not welding — he says 'the crack is removed, so no repair is needed.' Evaluate this approach.

Grade on: Grinding out a crack without subsequent welding creates a gouged area (local metal loss); the gouged area must be evaluated per API 579 FFS as a local thinned area (LTA) or groove-type flaw — the remaining thickness after grinding must exceed the minimum required thickness; if it does not, weld repair is mandatory; additionally, grinding alone does not address the root cause of the crack (what caused the crack to form and will it reform?); if the crack was caused by SCC or HIC, simply removing the crack without addressing the corrosive mechanism means the crack will recur; after grinding, PT or MT of the ground area is required to confirm complete removal; if the remaining thickness is below minimum, weld fill repair per ASME PCC-2 is required.
Mechanical QC
practical

A pressure vessel shell has the following data: Material SA-516 Gr.70, allowable stress S = 137.9 MPa, joint efficiency E = 1.0, corrosion allowance CA = 3 mm, inside radius R = 600 mm, design pressure P = 20 bar (2 MPa). Calculate the minimum required shell thickness per ASME VIII UG-27(c)(1) and determine whether a measured shell thickness of 20 mm is acceptable with 3 mm corrosion allowance already applied.

Grade on: Formula: t = (P × R) / (S × E − 0.6 × P) = (2 × 600) / (137.9 × 1.0 − 0.6 × 2) = 1200 / (137.9 − 1.2) = 1200 / 136.7 = 8.78 mm. Minimum thickness (including CA) = 8.78 + 3 = 11.78 mm. Measured thickness 20 mm (this is the current measured thickness with 3 mm CA already applied from the calculation perspective) — wait, re-read: 'with 3 mm CA already applied' means 20 mm is the remaining structural thickness after 3 mm corrosion = 17 mm effective structural, OR 20 mm is the measured thickness and CA is additional. Assuming 20 mm is current measured = 20 mm − 3 mm CA = 17 mm effective > 8.78 mm required — ACCEPTABLE. Candidate must demonstrate the calculation correctly and compare correctly.
Mechanical QC
practical

A pump alignment report shows the following cold laser alignment readings: Horizontal offset: +0.15 mm at coupling OD 150 mm; Vertical offset: −0.08 mm; Horizontal angularity: +0.03 mm/100 mm; Vertical angularity: −0.05 mm/100 mm. Specification: offset ≤ 0.05 mm, angularity ≤ 0.05 mm/100 mm. Evaluate each parameter and state what corrections are needed.

Grade on: (1) Horizontal offset: 0.15 mm > 0.05 mm maximum — FAIL; pump must be moved horizontally to reduce offset to ≤0.05 mm; (2) Vertical offset: 0.08 mm > 0.05 mm — FAIL; add shims under pump feet to raise pump; (3) Horizontal angularity: 0.03 mm/100 mm < 0.05 mm — PASS; (4) Vertical angularity: 0.05 mm/100 mm = exactly at limit — PASS (borderline — note for monitoring). Summary: two parameters out of specification (horizontal and vertical offset); corrections required before pump can be accepted for commissioning.

A PRV on a gas separator has a set pressure of 80 bar and a maximum allowable accumulated pressure of 110% of set pressure (88 bar) for a single PRV installation per ASME VIII. During a process simulation, the maximum calculated overpressure scenario is 91 bar for a fire case. Evaluate whether the single PRV installation meets the code requirements.

Grade on: For fire case per ASME VIII: maximum accumulated pressure = 121% of set pressure = 1.21 × 80 = 96.8 bar for a fire case with a single PRV; the calculated overpressure for the fire case is 91 bar; 91 bar < 96.8 bar allowable for fire case → ACCEPTABLE for the fire case. For normal overpressure scenarios (non-fire): maximum accumulated pressure = 110% × 80 = 88 bar. The candidate should note that the 91 bar calculated scenario must be confirmed as a 'fire case' only — if any non-fire scenario results in 91 bar, it would fail the 88 bar (110%) limit. Based on the given data (fire case), the installation is acceptable.

Review the following PRV bench test data and state the pass/fail determination per API 527 for each PRV: PRV A: Set pressure 50 bar, opens at 51 bar, reseats at 45 bar; PRV B: Set pressure 100 bar, opens at 103 bar, reseats at 95 bar; PRV C: Set pressure 25 bar, opens at 24 bar (below set pressure), reseats at 22 bar.

Grade on: PRV A: Set pressure 50 bar, opens at 51 bar — 51/50 = 102% — within +3% (to 51.5 bar) for set ≤ 70 bar; reseat at 45 bar — blowdown = (51-45)/50 = 12% > 7% maximum — FAIL on blowdown; PRV B: opens at 103 bar — 103/100 = 103% — within +3% for set > 70 bar (to 103 bar) — PASS on set pressure; reseat at 95 bar — blowdown = (103-95)/100 = 8% > 7% — FAIL on blowdown; PRV C: opens at 24 bar — below set pressure of 25 bar — FAIL (PRV opens too early; simmer detected below set pressure). Summary: PRV A and B fail on blowdown; PRV C fails on premature opening.

A storage tank API 653 inspection report shows the following shell thickness measurements for Course 1 (lowest course): Average measured thickness = 11.2 mm; Minimum measured point = 9.8 mm; Original nominal thickness = 12.7 mm; Corrosion rate = 0.25 mm/yr; Required minimum thickness per API 653 for this course = 8.5 mm. Calculate remaining life, next inspection interval, and allowable inspection date.

Grade on: Remaining life = (minimum measured − minimum required) / corrosion rate = (9.8 − 8.5) / 0.25 = 1.3 / 0.25 = 5.2 years; Next inspection interval per API 653 = 50% of remaining life = 2.6 years; Maximum interval per API 653 = 5 years (10-year external max); So next inspection due in 2.6 years. If this inspection was performed in 2025, next inspection is due by approximately mid-2028. Candidate must apply the correct formula and identify the limiting inspection interval.

Review the following mechanical completion checklist for a centrifugal pump and identify all items that are nonconforming or require attention before commissioning: (a) Motor rotation direction: Verified — CCW (pump requires CW); (b) Coupling guard: Not installed; (c) Bearing oil level: Visible in sight glass; (d) Seal flush plan: API 682 Plan 11 connected; (e) Foundation hold-down bolts: Hand-tight; (f) Motor nameplate: 90 kW, 2,950 RPM, 380 V; pump data sheet: 90 kW, 2,950 RPM, 415 V.

Grade on: (a) Motor rotation CCW vs. required CW — FAIL — rotation direction must be corrected (swap 2 of 3 motor power phases) before coupling; (b) Coupling guard not installed — FAIL — mandatory safety device; cannot run without coupling guard; (c) Bearing oil level visible — PASS; (d) Seal flush plan connected — PASS; (e) Foundation bolts hand-tight — FAIL — bolts must be torqued to specification per API 686 before alignment or start-up; (f) Motor 380 V vs. 415 V pump data sheet — investigate: is the pump data sheet wrong or the motor supply wrong? This is a voltage discrepancy requiring resolution before energisation. Summary: four nonconformances: rotation direction, coupling guard, torque, voltage mismatch.

A fired heater tube inspection UT report shows the following thickness readings (mm) at the hot zone of tube T-22 (original nominal wall 10 mm, minimum required 7.5 mm): Top: 9.2; Bottom: 8.5; East: 10.1; West: 5.8. Evaluate the readings and state the finding.

Grade on: Reading analysis: Top 9.2 mm — above minimum (7.5 mm) — PASS; Bottom 8.5 mm — above minimum — PASS; East 10.1 mm — above minimum — PASS; West 5.8 mm — BELOW minimum (5.8 < 7.5 mm) — FAIL; The tube has localised wall thinning at the west position (5.8 mm) that is below the 7.5 mm minimum. This tube must be replaced before the heater is returned to service. The position (west side = facing a specific burner) suggests possible localised flame impingement — investigate flame pattern adjustment. Note: The minimum of all four readings determines the tube condition, and any reading below minimum requires action.

Review this heat exchanger tube ECT summary for a 20-year-old cooling water heat exchanger (125 tubes total): No significant wall loss (< 20%): 92 tubes; 20–40% wall loss: 18 tubes; 40–60% wall loss: 9 tubes; 60–80% wall loss: 4 tubes; >80% wall loss: 2 tubes. Current total plugged tubes: 0. Evaluate the bundle condition and state your recommendation.

Grade on: Tube condition assessment: 2 tubes with >80% wall loss — IMMEDIATE plugging required (remaining wall < 2 mm on a 10 mm tube — perforation risk); 4 tubes with 60–80% wall loss — should be plugged before return to service (approaching perforation); 9 tubes with 40–60% wall loss — consider plugging (close to recommended 40% threshold); 18 tubes with 20–40% wall loss — monitor, plan plugging at next opportunity; Percentage of tubes pluggable: 2+4 = 6 tubes must be plugged minimum = 6/125 = 4.8%; TEMA allows up to 10% tube plugging before recommending bundle replacement; Recommendation: plug the 6 tubes with >60% wall loss; monitor 40–60% group at next inspection; evaluate tube bundle replacement in 2–3 years given age and extent of deterioration.

A vibration spectrum for a 3,000 RPM centrifugal pump shows dominant peaks at: 50 Hz (1X running speed), 100 Hz (2X), and 12.5 Hz (0.25X sub-harmonic). The 0.25X sub-harmonic has an amplitude of 5 mm/s vs. the 1X amplitude of 3 mm/s. What does the 0.25X sub-harmonic most likely indicate and what action is required?

Grade on: 0.25X (quarter-speed frequency) is a relatively unusual sub-harmonic; at 12.5 Hz for a 3,000 RPM (50 Hz) pump: this frequency is unlikely to be a simple bearing or fluid dynamic effect; possible causes: (1) Rubs at 0.25X can indicate a partial rub (intermittent contact at 4 cycles per revolution); (2) Acoustic resonance in suction or discharge piping; (3) Hydraulic pulsation at sub-synchronous frequency; The relatively high amplitude of the sub-harmonic (5 mm/s > 1X amplitude of 3 mm/s) is unusual and concerning — it suggests the sub-harmonic is a significant dynamic event, not background noise; Required action: further vibration analysis (spectrum, time waveform, phase analysis), inspection of pump internals for rub marks, piping acoustic resonance assessment; consider shutdown for inspection if the amplitude is increasing.
Mechanical QC
practical

A pressure vessel FFS assessment per API 579 Level 1 for a local thinned area (LTA) requires the average measured thickness ≥ (0.8 × t_min). The vessel minimum required thickness t_min = 10 mm. The LTA dimensions are 200 mm × 150 mm. The thickness measurements within the LTA are: 8.5, 9.0, 8.8, 9.2, 7.8, 8.9, 9.5, 8.1 mm. Calculate the average thickness and determine whether the LTA passes Level 1 screening.

Grade on: Average thickness = (8.5 + 9.0 + 8.8 + 9.2 + 7.8 + 8.9 + 9.5 + 8.1) / 8 = 69.8 / 8 = 8.725 mm. Threshold for Level 1 = 0.8 × t_min = 0.8 × 10 = 8.0 mm. Average 8.725 mm > 8.0 mm threshold — PASSES Level 1 screening. However: the minimum individual reading is 7.8 mm — check if the minimum individual thickness must also meet t_min (10 mm) for absolute fitness; per API 579 Level 1, if average meets the 0.8t_min criterion and the point minimum is above (t_min − CA), typically the LTA passes. Note that 7.8 mm < t_min of 10 mm — the individual minimum would trigger further assessment. Candidate should recognise that Level 1 uses average but minimum individual must also be considered.

Evaluate the following pump cold alignment record (laser alignment, soft-foot corrected) and specify the corrective shim changes needed: Current readings: Vertical angularity: +0.08 mm/100 mm (Motor feet 1&2 high relative to pump). Horizontal angularity: 0.00 mm/100 mm. Vertical offset: +0.12 mm (Motor shaft high relative to pump). Horizontal offset: −0.05 mm. Specification: angularity ≤ 0.05 mm/100 mm; offset ≤ 0.05 mm.

Grade on: Non-conforming values: Vertical angularity 0.08 > 0.05 limit — FAIL; Vertical offset 0.12 > 0.05 limit — FAIL; Horizontal angularity 0.00 — PASS; Horizontal offset 0.05 = at limit — PASS (borderline). Correction for vertical: both motor shaft high (offset) and motor far-end high relative to pump (angularity) — need to remove shims from motor feet; specifically: to correct both angularity and offset simultaneously, calculate shim changes at each motor foot using the standard two-foot correction formula; the motor near feet need shims removed to bring shaft down and correct the angularity; precise amount requires knowing the coupling to motor foot distances (not provided). State the principle clearly: reduce shims at both motor feet with emphasis on near-end feet to correct angularity, and uniform reduction to address offset.

Review the following ASME VIII pressure vessel data report (U-1 form data) and identify discrepancies: Vessel service: Propylene storage; Design pressure: 24 bar; Design temperature: 55°C; Material: SA-516 Gr.55; Joint efficiency: 0.7 (spot RT); Shell thickness: 20 mm; Inside diameter: 1,500 mm; Corrosion allowance: 3 mm; MAWP stated on nameplate: 28 bar.

Grade on: Issue 1: Material SA-516 Gr.55 — SA-516 Grade designations are 55, 60, 65, and 70 — Grade 55 has allowable stress of approximately 103 MPa at ambient temperature (lower than Grade 70 at 137.9 MPa); this is unusual for propylene service (typically Grade 70 is used); verify against design intent; Issue 2: MAWP stated as 28 bar > design pressure of 24 bar — verify calculation: t_min = P × R / (S × E − 0.6P); with SA-516 Gr.55 S≈103 MPa, E=0.7, R=750 mm: t_min = 24 × 10^5 Pa × 0.75 / (103×10^6 × 0.7 − 0.6×24×10^5) = 18/72.1-1.44 = 18/70.66 ≈ 0.025 m = 25 mm; structural thickness available = 20 − 3 = 17 mm < 25 mm required — this suggests the vessel is UNDERSIZED for the stated conditions; the calculation must be fully verified with exact material allowable stress and design conditions.
Mechanical QC
practical

A spring-loaded PRV has a set pressure of 120 bar. Calculate the maximum back pressure allowed for: (a) a conventional spring-loaded PRV; (b) a balanced-bellows PRV. For (a), state what happens to the PRV performance above this limit.

Grade on: (a) Conventional PRV maximum back pressure = 10% of set pressure = 0.10 × 120 = 12 bar; above 12 bar back pressure, the conventional PRV will have reduced lift (the downstream pressure partially opposes the spring, requiring higher inlet pressure to achieve full lift), leading to reduced flow capacity and potential chatter; (b) Balanced-bellows PRV — the bellows cancels the effect of back pressure on the spring; maximum back pressure typically 50% of set pressure = 0.50 × 120 = 60 bar; the balanced bellows maintains consistent lift regardless of back pressure up to 50% of set. The candidate must demonstrate understanding of both PRV types and the effect of back pressure.
Mechanical QC
practical

During a storage tank bottom MFL survey, the technician reports 'Severity 3' indications over a 2 m × 3 m area of the tank bottom, and 'Severity 4' indications at three discrete locations of approximately 100 mm × 100 mm each. The tank bottom nominal plate thickness is 8 mm and minimum required per API 653 is 5 mm. Describe the follow-up inspection and disposition process.

Grade on: MFL follow-up: Severity 3 indications (50–80% wall loss estimated) — spot UT at minimum 10 representative points within the 2 m × 3 m zone to confirm MFL severity classification and establish actual remaining thickness; Severity 4 indications (>80% wall loss estimated) — spot UT at each of the three locations; Disposition: any UT reading < 5 mm minimum required → repair required; Severity 4 at 8 mm nominal: 80% loss = 1.6 mm remaining (< 5 mm → repair mandatory); Severity 3 at 8 mm nominal: 65% average loss = 2.8 mm remaining (< 5 mm → repair mandatory if confirmed by UT); Repair methods: small areas (< 300 mm diameter) — weld patch per API 653; larger areas — plate replacement; vacuum box test of all repair welds.

practical

A fired heater duty calculation shows that the required heat duty is 10 MW at 85% thermal efficiency. The heater is supplied with natural gas having a lower heating value (LHV) of 50 MJ/kg. The burner design requires a natural gas flow rate of 235 kg/hr. Verify whether the supplied gas flow rate matches the required heat duty.

Grade on: Required heat input = Required heat duty / thermal efficiency = 10 MW / 0.85 = 11.76 MW = 11.76 MJ/s. Heat input per hour = 11.76 × 3600 = 42,353 MJ/hr. Gas flow rate required = Heat input / LHV = 42,353 MJ/hr / 50 MJ/kg = 847 kg/hr. Supplied flow rate = 235 kg/hr. 235 kg/hr << 847 kg/hr required — the supplied gas flow rate is only 28% of what is required; the heater will be severely underperforming; investigate: Is the burner design flow rate 235 kg/hr per burner (multiple burners) or total? If there are 4 burners at 235 kg/hr each = 940 kg/hr, which is close to 847 kg/hr. Candidate should flag the apparent discrepancy and clarify whether 235 kg/hr is per burner or total.

practical

Review a mechanical run test data sheet for a centrifugal pump (API 610): Design flow: 450 m³/hr; Design head: 120 m; Design speed: 2,970 RPM; Design efficiency: 78%; Measured test results at design flow: Head 118 m; Speed 2,970 RPM; Efficiency 75%; Vibration: 3.8 mm/s RMS. API 610 acceptance criteria: head within −3% to +8% of rated; efficiency within −2 percentage points of rated; vibration ≤ 4.5 mm/s. Evaluate each parameter.

Grade on: (1) Head: rated 120 m; measured 118 m; deviation = (118−120)/120 = −1.7%; allowed: −3% to +8%; −1.7% is within −3% limit — PASS; (2) Efficiency: rated 78%; measured 75%; deviation = −3 percentage points; allowed −2 points; −3 points > −2 points — FAIL; (3) Vibration: 3.8 mm/s < 4.5 mm/s limit — PASS. Summary: pump FAILS on efficiency (75% vs. 78% rated, −3 points vs. −2 points allowed); investigation of internal clearances, impeller trim, or wearing rings required. Head and vibration PASS.

A heat exchanger shell is to be re-rated from 25 bar to 30 bar at 200°C using SA-516 Gr.70. Current measured wall thickness = 22 mm; corrosion allowance = 2 mm; effective thickness = 20 mm; inside radius = 400 mm; allowable stress at 200°C = 131 MPa; E = 1.0. Calculate the minimum required thickness at the new MAWP of 30 bar (3 MPa) and determine if re-rating is acceptable.

Grade on: Formula: t_min = P × R / (S × E − 0.6 × P) = 3 × 400 / (131 × 1.0 − 0.6 × 3) = 1200 / (131 − 1.8) = 1200 / 129.2 = 9.29 mm. With CA of 2 mm: t_min total = 9.29 + 2 = 11.29 mm. Effective available thickness = 20 mm (measured 22 mm − 2 mm CA). 20 mm > 11.29 mm — the shell is ACCEPTABLE for re-rating to 30 bar. A hydrostatic test at 1.3 × 30 = 39 bar (or 1.5 × 30 = 45 bar per older editions) would then be required to complete the re-rating process.
Mechanical QC
practical

During a heat exchanger pre-commissioning water flush, the flushing water from the tube-side outlet is visually milky and shows pH of 4.5. The heat exchanger is a new CS shell-and-tube unit. Evaluate the cause of the discoloured, acidic flush water and state what action is required.

Grade on: Milky, acidic (pH 4.5) flush water from a new CS tube-side indicates: (1) Mill scale and rust removal by the flush water — initial flushes from new CS equipment are often discoloured with iron oxides; (2) The pH 4.5 is acidic and unusual for plain water flush — possible source: residual acid from chemical cleaning (pickling) not properly neutralised; or contaminated flush water source; (3) Milky appearance could also indicate a small tube leak if shell-side fluid was incompatible; Action required: (1) Continue flushing until water runs clear and pH is neutral (6.5–7.5); (2) Verify flush water source pH (confirm source water is not acidic); (3) If pH does not recover after extended flushing, investigate whether pickling acid was used and not neutralised; (4) Do not proceed to service until flushing water is clear and neutral.

practical

You receive a pressure vessel completion package for a new ASME VIII Div.1 vessel. Review the following completion summary and identify all deficiencies before signing the mechanical completion certificate: (a) ASME U-1 form: Not included in package; (b) Hydrostatic test record: Included, test at 1.3 × MAWP = 65 bar; (c) PWHT record: Not applicable (CS, wall ≤ 38 mm, no P91); (d) RT of all seam welds: 10% spot RT performed (E=0.85 joint efficiency); (e) PRV functional test: Not included; (f) Nameplate rubbing: Included; (g) Final VT sign-off: Not included.

Grade on: (a) ASME U-1 form missing — FAIL — mandatory document; (b) Hydrostatic test at 1.3 × MAWP — acceptable per current ASME VIII edition (vs. older 1.5×); verify test temp above MDMT + 10°C — PASS on value but verify temp; (c) PWHT N/A for CS ≤ 38 mm — depends on service (sour service? requires PWHT per SAES even below 38 mm); flag for verification; (d) 10% RT with E=0.85 — acceptable per ASME VIII UW-12 for spot RT joint efficiency 0.85; (e) PRV functional test not included — FAIL if a PRV is part of the vessel code scope; (f) Nameplate rubbing included — PASS; (g) Final VT sign-off not included — FAIL. Summary: three items missing (U-1 form, PRV functional test, final VT sign-off) — package cannot be signed until complete.

A static equipment mechanical QC audit of a fabrication shop reveals the following findings. Evaluate each and classify as NCR (major), Observation (minor), or Acceptable: (a) A pressure vessel being fabricated shows a 15 mm misalignment between two shell courses at a long seam weld, before welding. (b) Mill scale visible on inside of vessel shell before internal coating application. (c) A fitter is using an unapproved grinder for weld preparation on P5A (chrome-moly) pipe. (d) The calibration tag on the torque wrench used for nameplate bolting is 3 months past expiry. (e) A 316L SS nozzle is temporarily stored in direct contact with a carbon steel surface.

Grade on: (a) 15 mm shell course misalignment — ASME VIII UW-33 limits longitudinal seam alignment mismatch; for plates > 12.7 mm, limit is the lesser of 1/4T or 3.2 mm; 15 mm >> 3.2 mm — MAJOR NCR; (b) Mill scale inside vessel — should be removed before internal coating per coating specification — MINOR OBSERVATION or NCR depending on coating spec requirements; flag as NCR if coating specification prohibits mill scale; (c) Unapproved grinder on P5A pipe — weld preparation tools on chrome-moly must be controlled to prevent contamination; use of unapproved tools on alloy pipe is an NCR per SAES-W-011 tool segregation requirements; (d) Expired torque wrench calibration — all calibrated tools must have current calibration; expired calibration = NCR (minor but documented); (e) SS contact with CS surface — risk of iron contamination causing surface rust on 316L in service; NCR for material contamination prevention.
Electrical QC
mcq

During incoming inspection of a motor control centre (MCC) at a gas processing plant, the QC Inspector verifies the IP rating of the enclosure. The area is classified as Zone 1, gas group IIA, temperature class T3. The MCC enclosure is rated IP54. Is this acceptable for outdoor installation in a Zone 1 classified area?

Yes — IP54 provides adequate protection against dust and splash, which is sufficient for outdoor classified areas.
No — Zone 1 locations require Ex d (flameproof) or Ex e (increased safety) equipment with the appropriate group and temperature class certification, IP54 alone is not an ignition protection classification and does not qualify the MCC for Zone 1 installation.
Yes — IP54 is the minimum required for outdoor classified areas per SAES-P-111.
No — Zone 1 requires IP65 minimum, IP54 is only acceptable for Zone 2.

No — Zone 1 locations require Ex d (flameproof) or Ex e (increased safety) equipment with the appropriate group and temperature class certification, IP54 alone is not an ignition protection classification and does not qualify the MCC for Zone 1 installation.

IP ratings (IEC 60529) describe ingress protection against solid objects and water — they are NOT explosion protection classifications. Equipment in Zone 1 must carry IECEx or ATEX certification with the appropriate protection concept (Ex d, Ex e, Ex p, etc.), gas group (IIA, IIB, IIC), and temperature class (T1–T6). An MCC in Zone 1 requires Ex e (increased safety) or Ex d certification, not merely IP54.

mcq

A 33 kV substation cable termination is found to have been installed without stress control grading at the cable end. The cable is XLPE insulated with a metallic screen. What is the primary risk of missing the stress cone/stress grading?

The cable will have higher resistivity at the termination, reducing power transfer efficiency.
Electric field concentration at the cable screen cut-back point will cause insulation failure by partial discharge and eventual dielectric breakdown at the termination.

An electrical QC Inspector witnesses a HiPot (high-potential dielectric withstand) test on a new 6.6 kV cable. The test voltage applied is 20 kV DC for 15 minutes. During the test, the leakage current starts at 2 μA and increases to 45 μA over the 15-minute period. What does this trend indicate?

Normal behaviour — leakage current always increases during a DC HiPot test due to absorption current effects.
Concern — a rapidly increasing leakage current (2 μA to 45 μA) during a DC HiPot test indicates a defective or degraded insulation, good insulation shows a decreasing leakage current over time (absorption current diminishes), increasing leakage current indicates a conduction path developing through the insulation, the test should be stopped to prevent insulation failure and the cable should be investigated.
Acceptable — the leakage current must be compared only to the maximum allowable value, not the trend.
Normal — the increase is due to temperature rise of the cable during the test increasing conductivity.

Concern — a rapidly increasing leakage current (2 μA to 45 μA) during a DC HiPot test indicates a defective or degraded insulation, good insulation shows a decreasing leakage current over time (absorption current diminishes), increasing leakage current indicates a conduction path developing through the insulation, the test should be stopped to prevent insulation failure and the cable should be investigated.

During a DC HiPot test, leakage current through good insulation follows three phases: initial transient (capacitive charging, decays quickly), absorption (polarisation, decays slowly), and steady conduction (constant low value). Increasing leakage current indicates either insulation breakdown is in progress or a conduction path (moisture, contamination, void breakdown) is developing. The test should be stopped — continuing risks completing the insulation failure.

The SAES-P-111 earthing and bonding requirements for a classified area in a gas processing plant include bonding of all metallic equipment and piping. Describe the inspection programme for verifying that all bonding and earthing connections are correctly installed and meet resistance requirements.

Grade on: Visual inspection — check that all bonding jumpers are installed at every mechanical joint in classified areas (flanges, unions, pipe-to-equipment transitions); check bond conductor size (typically 10 mm² Cu per SAES-P-111); check crimp quality and connection point (not painted surface — bare metal contact required); bonding connection at each equipment item (vessels, pumps, compressors) to earth electrode; Resistance testing — bond resistance at each joint (typically < 1 Ω); earth resistance of each equipment item (< 5 Ω per SAES-P-111 general requirement); earth mat resistance for each hazardous area substation; Record keeping — bonding inspection register with location, conductor size, resistance measurement, date, and inspector signature.

Describe what a 'partial discharge' (PD) test is for HV cables and switchgear, why it is performed before energisation, and what acceptance criteria are used.

Grade on: Partial discharge (PD) — localised electrical discharges in voids, contaminants, or sharp protrusions within the insulation system that do not bridge the full insulation but cause progressive insulation erosion; PD test methods: acoustic (ultrasonic detection for GIS), UHF (ultra-high frequency for GIS), IEC 60270 (conventional PD measurement in pC for cables and switchgear); Why before energisation: PD present at rated voltage in a new system indicates manufacturing or installation defects (cable joint quality, switchgear contamination); these will progress to full insulation failure; Acceptance criteria: IEC 60840 cable — PD extinction voltage > 1.5 U0, PD level < 10 pC at 1.73 U0; GIS — PD free at rated voltage or < 5 pC depending on standard; significance: a PD-free acceptance test significantly increases confidence in long-term reliability.

essay
Explain the hazards associated with arc flash in electrical switchgear and describe the inspection programme elements that can reduce arc flash risk.

Grade on: Arc flash hazards — an arc fault in switchgear releases energy in the form of intense light (UV, IR, visible), heat (copper vaporises at arc temperatures ~20,000 K), pressure wave, and shrapnel; arc flash can cause severe burns, blindness, hearing loss, and fatalities; arc flash energy (calories/cm²) determines required PPE level; Inspection programme to reduce arc flash risk: verify protection relay settings are optimised for fast fault clearing (faster clearing = less arc flash energy); verify all bus connections are tight (thermography programme); maintain proper door/cover closure; implement electrical PPE programme per NFPA 70E; install arc flash labels on all equipment (arc flash hazard analysis per IEEE 1584); install arc flash detection relays (ultra-fast optical or overcurrent-based) on critical switchgear; restrict live-work to trained personnel.

essay
An ARAMCO new project requires all Ex-rated electrical equipment to be certified and traceable. Describe the incoming inspection checklist for IECEx/ATEX-certified equipment received on site.

Grade on: Certificate verification — check IECEx or ATEX certificate number against the IECEx/ATEX certificate database; verify equipment group (I, II, IIA, IIB, IIC), category (1G/2G/3G or 1D/2D/3D), temperature class (T1–T6), and protection concept (Ex d, Ex e, Ex p, Ex i, Ex n, Ex t); check certificate validity (some certificates have expiry dates); compare certificate to equipment nameplate (must match); Physical inspection — check nameplate is complete (zone, group, T-class, certificate number, manufacturer); check enclosure for damage (flameproof enclosures must not have cracks or deformation); check cable entry (Ex e glands must be correctly sized and cable must clamp within the specified range); check cable gland certification; check that no field modifications have been made that would invalidate the certificate; Record — issue equipment certificate register in the QC documentation package.

Describe the quality control requirements for the installation and testing of a cathodic protection (CP) rectifier and anode groundbed at a new buried pipeline.

Grade on: CP rectifier installation — verify rectifier voltage/current output range matches design (CP design current and voltage); verify DC positive connected to anode groundbed, negative connected to pipeline (critical — reverse polarity would accelerate corrosion instead of protecting); verify rectifier transformer fuse rating and disconnect switch; Anode groundbed installation — check depth and spacing of anodes per design; verify anode-to-soil contact (backfill quality, moisture); verify anode lead wire insulation integrity (IR test on anode leads before backfill); Pipeline connection — verify test post installation at design spacing; verify isolation flange joints (continuity test across flange — must show break); CP system testing — pipe-to-soil potential measurement at all test posts; minimum protected potential per NACE SP0169 (typically −850 mV CSE for CS); rectifier adjustment to achieve protection potential; record all readings.

You are responsible for electrical QC on an offshore oil platform. An emergency has occurred — a feeder cable to the main fire pump has failed by insulation breakdown during testing. The fire pump is safety-critical. Describe your immediate response and the steps to restore the fire pump to service.

Grade on: Immediate response — notify platform safety officer; verify fire water system is still operable via alternate supply if available (diesel fire pump?); isolate failed cable safely (LOTO); Emergency cable replacement — using emergency cable procurement; interim: if fire pump can be connected via temporary cable of correct rating (check cable size, voltage rating, and routing), implement with supervisor approval and formal risk assessment; Permanent fix: measure failed cable section (IR test to locate fault; if fault is localised, consider joint or partial replacement); full cable replacement may be required; Testing before re-energisation — full IR test, continuity, earth loop impedance; Protection relay — verify protection is set correctly for the new cable; Documentation — NCR for cable failure, report to ARAMCO maintenance authority, root cause analysis (manufacturing defect, installation damage, test over-voltage).

Describe the commissioning verification requirements for an Automatic Transfer Switch (ATS) that transfers electrical supply from a utility source to a standby generator in a hospital-grade critical power system.

Grade on: ATS testing sequence: Confirm normal source voltage and frequency are within window; Simulate utility source failure (drop voltage below threshold) — verify ATS starts generator; Verify generator starts within required time (typically < 10 seconds for critical systems); Verify ATS transfers load to generator after confirmed generator stable voltage and frequency; Verify ATS timer functions (transfer delay, re-transfer delay after utility restoration); Test each individual timer setting; Test ATS retransfer when utility restores; Test ATS inhibit function (maintenance bypass); Test ATS in closed-transition or open-transition mode per design; Test generator under rated load for minimum 2 hours; Record all timer values and compare against specification; Verify neutral switching (4-pole ATS) if applicable; Verify bypass switch function.

An ARAMCO cable tray installation inspection on a process plant reveals that the cable fill in several trays exceeds 50% of the tray cross-sectional area. Explain why cable fill limits exist, what the technical consequences of exceeding these limits are, and what corrective action is required.

Grade on: Cable fill limits — NEC 392.22 and SAES-P-104 limit cable fill in trays to manage cable heat dissipation; when cables are closely packed, each cable's heat output raises the temperature of adjacent cables (mutual heating), reducing the current-carrying capacity of all cables; at >40–50% fill (depending on cable type), cables must be derated per NEC ampacity correction tables; Technical consequences: exceeding fill causes cables to operate at above-rated temperature, accelerating insulation ageing, reducing insulation life, and increasing fault risk; Corrective actions: option 1 — install additional cable trays to redistribute cables; option 2 — derate all cables in the affected tray and verify that the derated ampacity still meets the circuit design current; in most cases, derating below the circuit design current requires physical reduction in cable fill (additional trays).

A new ARAMCO solar photovoltaic (PV) power system is being installed to supplement site power. Describe the electrical QC inspection activities for the PV system, from module installation through DC and AC system testing and grid connection.

Grade on: Module installation — verify module orientation (azimuth and tilt angle per design); module nameplate vs. specification; MC4 connector inspection (proper crimping, no exposed conductors, rated for outdoor/UV use); mounting system torque check; String wiring — verify string polarity (+ to + and − to −) before energisation; string open-circuit voltage (Voc) and short-circuit current (Isc) measurements per string (compare with expected values for number of modules and irradiance); DC cabling — cable rating vs. maximum string voltage; DC isolators; Combiner box — fuse ratings, SPD (surge protection device) installation; DC earth fault monitoring; Inverter — verify inverter DC input voltage vs. PV Voc, anti-islanding protection setting; AC connection — power quality measurements (THD, voltage); grid protection relay settings (over/under voltage, over/under frequency); commissioning test: ramp from zero load to full load, record DC and AC efficiency.

Describe the inspection requirements and testing methods for a high-voltage (33 kV) power transformer during site installation, before it is energised for the first time at a remote ARAMCO facility.

Grade on: Physical inspection on arrival — check for shipping damage; verify oil level and conservator; check oil sampling (DGA — dissolved gas analysis baseline); check all bushings for cracks; Electrical tests before energisation: winding resistance (all taps, check for temperature correction); TTR (transformer turns ratio) at all taps; insulation resistance (IR) — all windings, windings to earth, HV to LV; dielectric absorption ratio (DAR) or polarisation index (PI); power factor/tan delta if required by specification; vector group verification; No-load test (energise at rated voltage, measure no-load current and losses); On-load test (apply load, measure winding temperature); Buchholz relay functional test; OLTC operation test; Oil dielectric strength test (breakdown voltage per IEC 60156); DGA after initial energisation (24 hours); Protection relay commissioning.

You are reviewing the electrical IFC (Issued For Construction) drawings for a new LNG facility and identify that the cable schedule shows 16 mm² cables supplying motors rated 37 kW at 415V over cable runs of 80 metres, with no voltage drop calculation provided. Describe your approach to raising this technical concern and the engineering resolution process.

Grade on: Technical concern identification — perform voltage drop calculation: I (37 kW at 415V, 0.85 PF) = 37,000 / (1.732 × 415 × 0.85) ≈ 60.5 A; V_drop = 1.732 × 60.5 × 0.080 km × 1.15 Ω/km (for 16 mm² Cu) = 9.7 V = 2.3% of 415 V — this is within 5% limit, suggesting the cable may be adequate; however also check: ampacity of 16 mm² Cu (per IEC 60364-5-52, approximately 76 A in free air — borderline for 60.5 A in tray); Raise concern via formal Design Query / Engineering Clarification (EQ/EC) to the EPC electrical engineer; include calculation showing the concern; engineer must respond with formal calculation and clarification; if cable is confirmed undersized, issue an NCR on the IFC drawing and require revised cable schedule before construction continues; document resolution in the quality record.

A safety officer asks you to explain, in plain language, the difference between ATEX Zone 1 and Zone 2 areas and how equipment selection differs for each.

Grade on: Zone 1 — flammable gases or vapours are likely to be present occasionally in normal operation (normal operating releases, maintenance releases); Zone 2 — flammable gases present only in abnormal conditions or for short periods; Equipment selection: Zone 2 minimum — Category 3G (Ex n, Ex e low risk) or higher; Zone 1 minimum — Category 2G (Ex d, Ex e, Ex m, Ex i — more robust protection concepts); Zone 1 equipment is acceptable in Zone 2 (overprotection is acceptable); Zone 2 equipment (Category 3G) must NOT be used in Zone 1. Gas group and temperature class must match the specific hazardous substance for both zones.
